entries.title: Nationals 3, Tigers 1: Game Recap
entries.summary: Washington took a 1-0 lead in the second on a long homer to right-center field by CJ Abrams.
entries.content:
By Dave Hogg

CJ Abrams hit a tiebreaking two-run homer and added a solo shot to give the Washington Nationals a 3-1 victory over the Detroit Tigers on Tuesday night.

The Nationals won for the seventh time in 10 games, while Detroit dropped to 2-5 in its last seven. The Tigers have scored exactly one run in all five losses, while scoring nine and 11 runs in the two wins.

Both teams are 74-84 with four games left in the season.

Jackson Kent (2-4) picked up the win in relief of Nationals opener Riley Cornelio. Kent pitched four innings, allowing one unearned run on six hits and two walks. Erik Tolman pitched the ninth for his fourth save.

Tigers starter Drew Anderson (5-7) took the loss, allowing three runs on five hits. He struck out five without walking a batter.

Washington took a 1-0 lead in the second on a long homer to right-center field by Abrams. That gave him 100 RBIs to go along with his 30 homer/30 stolen base season.

The Tigers tied the game in the sixth when Ben Malgeri scored on Kent's second wild pitch of the inning. Washington also missed two opportunities to turn double plays in the inning.

Abrams then hit a two-run homer in the seventh, his 33rd of the season, to end Anderson's night.

Up nextThe teams finish their three-game series on Wednesday afternoon with Tigers LHP Framber Valdez (10-11, 4.06) facing a yet-to-be-announced Nationals starter.

entries.title: Mystics 79, Sun 69: Game Recap
entries.summary: The Mystics stretched their lead over Dallas and New York (tied for seventh) to one game with two days remaining in the regular season.
entries.content:
Shakira Austin had 25 points and 13 rebounds to help the Washington Mystics beat the Connecticut Sun 79-69 on Tuesday night for their franchise-record 27th win of the season.

Washington (27-16) set the previous mark of 26 wins in 2019, en route to the franchise’s only WNBA championship.

The Mystics stretched their lead over Dallas and New York (tied for seventh) to one game with two days remaining in the regular season.

Diamond Miller led Connecticut (10-33) with 19 points. Leila Lacan and Raegan Beers scored 11 points apiece.

Washington used a 15-4 run to push its lead into double figures with 3:26 left in the third quarter and Cotie McMahon hit a 3 about 90 seconds later that made it 66-53.

McMahon had 13 points and Sonia Citron 12 for the Mystics.

Austin made a career-high 11 free throws, extended her single-season franchise record to 397 rebounds and had her 20th double-double this season. Austin and Kiki Iraiafen (22 double-doubles) are the first teammates in WNBA history with at least 20 double-doubles in the same season.

The Sun outrebounded Washington 43-34. The Mystics have outrebounded their opponents a WNBA-record 39 times this season.

entries.title: Flights Are Resuming at DCA After Runway Light Failure
entries.summary: A ground stop triggered delays and cancellations for hours Tuesday night.
entries.content:
A major runway was again open at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport after several flights were delayed or canceled Tuesday night when a lighting equipment failure forced the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a ground stop, according to DCA officials.

At around 10:20 p.m., officials announced that crews had restored the malfunctioning runway lights, but warned travelers to expect residual delays throughout the night.

According to FAA alerts, the lighting system on the airport's busiest and longest runway was not working, forcing authorities to issue significant delays.

The FAA halted all flights departing to DCA through 10:30 p.m., causing airlines to cancel over 43 flights, with departures delayed by about an hour on average, according to FlightAware.

This story has been updated with the reopening of DCA’s longest runway.

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Sept. 25)
entries.summary: Theatre Week begins, “The Firebird” takes flight and a Eurovision star lands at Black Cat.
entries.content:
Thursday

Theatre Week
Various DMV Theaters, $25 to $65, through Oct. 11

Over an 18-day stretch, 27 area theaters have blocked off a set number of seats at discount prices. Admittedly, 18 days is not a “week,” but to (loosely) quote the musical “Rent,” how do you measure a season of love? Should your first choice show at a larger theater sell out, Theatre Week is a great time to try a smaller local company. Free events include today’s pop-up serenades at Dulles and DCA, a concert at The Wharf on Sept. 29 and a “State of DC Theatre” podcast taping at Studio Theatre on Oct. 5.

“Lay Him Quietly” at Dance Place
3225 8th St. NE, 7 p.m. free, registration required

A decade ago, Dance Place hosted touring dance companies multiple times each month. Now, it’s only a few times a year, as the Brookland venue struggles with fiscal issues and leadership turnover. There’s a bright spot this Wednesday and Thursday, however, when the Swedish embassy presents a free immersive work by Hiroki Ichinose, a Japanese-American dance artist and member of Göteborg Operans Danskompani. Ichinose and fellow Swedish dancer Ninos Josef perform “Lay Him Quietly” before a film backdrop, a now-rare chance to see intimate international modern dance in the District.

More to explore: Photographer Sheila Pree Bright talks American flag imagery at the National Gallery of Art

Friday

All Things Go Music Festival 
Merriweather Post Pavilion, Columbia, tickets start at $170

Great news for anyone who has ever wanted to yell, “Summer isn’t over yet!” at the top of their lungs in late September: Swedish superstar and “Midnight Sun” singer Zara Larsson is among the headliners at this year’s All Things Go Music Festival. The 2026 lineup has more female boldfaced names than Lilith Fair. Mitski is the big draw on Friday, Hayley Williams and Larsson on Saturday and Brandi Carlile on Sunday.

Dance Theatre of Harlem at The National Theatre
1321 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, 7:30 (Also 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Saturday), $76 to $114

Washington Performing Arts first presented Dance Theatre of Harlem way back in 1973, four years after Arthur Mitchell founded his groundbreaking company dedicated to Black excellence in ballet. Given that a festival of Black dance was among the events cancelled at the Kennedy Center earlier this year, it’s all the more meaningful that WPA is welcoming Dance Theatre of Harlem back to town. The performance includes George Balanchine’s “Donizetti Variations,” a soulful suite set to music by Aretha Franklin and James Brown.

More to explore: IZIS at the Publick Playhouse

Saturday

MARO at The Black Cat
1811 14th St. NW, 7:30, $30

At every Eurovision Song Context, there’s a balladeer who’s too sincere to win the crystal trophy and confetti, but who wins over the crowd and launches an international career. In 2022 that act was MARO. For an easy-listening initiation, check out her dreamy cover of Harry Styles’ “As it Was” with Charlotte Cardin and November Ultra. Sadly, MARO’s spring North American tour was cancelled due to what the singer called “circumstances beyond our control.” That’s usually code for failure to secure a U.S. visa, all the better reason to turn out now that the Portuguese singer and her band made it to America.

Music From the Sole at George Mason University
4373 Mason Pond Drive, Fairfax, 7:30, $38 to $60, minors half price

Like dance? Got a car, or willing to spend time on public transit? Great, because it’s time to start schlepping to George Mason University if you want to see touring companies of Kennedy Center-caliber. The Center for the Arts’ 2026-27 dance season kicks off with Music From the Sole, a dance-and-music collective with Brazilian and Afro-Cuban influences, plus “flashes of samba, house, Lindy Hop and Orisha dances,” according to The New York Times review of “I Didn’t Come to Stay.” That’s the work they’ll perform here too, infused with a “party spirit” worth the drive to Fairfax.

More to explore: FiestaDC celebrates Latino Heritage Month on Pennsylvania Avenue.

Sunday 

Takoma Park Folk Festival
Takoma Park Middle School, 10:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., free

DMV neighborhood street fair season continues this weekend with a daylong celebration in The People’s Republic of Takoma Park, as some residents call their counter-culture enclave on the D.C.-Maryland border. The festival’s seven stages feature folk musicians, world music and children’s entertainment. There’s also a juried craft show, community tabling and two-dozen food vendors, most offering vegan and gluten-free options.

Black Women Make Movies at Shanklin Hall
2325 18th St. NW, 5 to 8 p.m, $23

Catch five short films at this event billed as a “screening + mixer” for “Black women filmmakers and the folx who love them.” Local documentaries in the lineup explore underground “numbers” gambling in the 1960s and “The Legacy of Lee’s Flower Shop,” one of D.C.’s oldest Black-owned businesses. Bonus: One drink is included with each ticket.

More to explore: Alexandria Symphony performs at the George Washington Masonic Memorial

entries.title: What to Expect From Xi’s Big Visit: Kicked Cans
entries.summary: Trump will roll out the red carpet for the Chinese leader, but current and former officials don’t envision big breakthroughs during the talks.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump will welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington for a state visit as the pair seeks to deepen their personal relationship and maintain some future stability.

The governments — which at times have been adversarial — have made slow progress on the tangible commitments agreed to in May when Trump visited Beijing. But the countries remain locked in strategic competitions bubbling beneath the surface of the leaders’ relationship. And it’s unlikely, according to experts and current and former U.S. officials who spoke with The Washington Sun, that a big breakthrough on the most profound sticking points will come during Xi’s visit.

“I think the status quo with China is not great by any stretch, but it's better than the alternative: a tariff war and a limited supply of our rare critical minerals,” said one U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak candidly. “So I think that the expectation is it's mostly going to be kicking the can.”

When Xi touches down Wednesday evening at Joint Base Andrews, it will kick off a couple of days of intense diplomacy. The world leaders last saw one another in May, when Trump traveled to Beijing for three days of events in which the Chinese regaled him with pomp and red carpets. That olive branch is expected to be reciprocated by the United States, which is preparing to pull out all the stops.

“The optics and the pageantry are really the point of this trip” — to show the strength of Xi and Trump’s relationship, Sara Schuman, a former senior U.S. negotiator for China trade and managing director at Beacon Global Strategies, told The Sun. The optics, she said, will likely “exceed the commercial deliverables.”

“The relationship is the circuit breaker that’s needed to manage the tensions beneath the surface, so they don’t break through,” Schuman said.

It’s expected to be an eventful summit — crammed with tours, military displays and meals — to fulfill Trump’s long-held desire to bring Xi back to Washington. Though Xi was in the United States in 2023, the Chinese leader’s last state visit was in 2015, during the Obama administration. It occurred coincidentally on the same dates — Sept. 24 and 25 — that he’ll visit with Trump.

Following Wednesday’s arrival ceremony, Trump and first lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife, Madam Peng Liyuan, at the White House on Thursday. They’ll hold a ceremony on the South Lawn and state floor, marked by 479 military personnel representing all branches of the U.S. military, according to the Office of the First Lady.

The Marine Band will play the Chinese and U.S. national anthems, and a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 Raptors will highlight a military display in a Rose Garden ceremony before a bilateral meeting takes place.

Trump and Xi are scheduled to address the crowd at Thursday evening’s state dinner. Prominent technology industry leaders are expected to attend, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and SpaceX and Tesla founder Elon Musk, according to a senior U.S. official.

NVIDIA AI Jensen Huang AP - 25301665725231 (4126x2751, AR: 1.50)
“The Chinese are reluctant to have top officials come to Washington for anything other than a state visit, and it has to be treated like it. It has something to do with their sense of protocol and standing. And so a state dinner is an essential component of a state visit, along with all the bells and whistles,” said Daniel R. Russel, who served as the assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during Xi’s 2015 state visit.

The summit will wrap up on Friday with a tour of the National Archives and America’s founding documents, after the Trumps host Xi and his wife for tea at the White House.

Not everyone favors the expected display of extravagance, including some of Trump's allies. Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) said in a floor speech on Tuesday that he “would have suggested the president not invite [Xi] to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States” if Trump had asked the senator, calling Xi a “brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator.”

The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

During Trump’s May trip to China, the leaders agreed to a one-year truce of sorts, called “strategic stability.” It aimed to prevent an escalation of tensions or a deliberate chokehold on critical commodities like U.S. export controls or China’s rare earth minerals. And that truce came with three broad agreements on issues central to the White House's goals.

U.S. officials said the two countries agreed to set up both a board of trade and a board of investments. The officials also said China would address Washington’s concerns over the supply chain for critical and rare earth minerals in addition to agreeing to purchase $17 billion worth of American agricultural products, prorated for 2026, in addition to commitments China had previously made to buy soybeans — a deal the Chinese said was never confirmed. And Trump said China had agreed to make an initial purchase of 200 American-made Boeing aircraft.

Of the three, the agreement to create a board of trade has seen the most significant movement, experts tracking the progress say. When first announced, the White House said in a document the board of trade would allow both countries “to manage bilateral trade across non-sensitive goods.” The U.S. set up a public comment period for the proposed board, a necessary step toward formally establishing it. And American officials seem poised to roll it out, coupled with some tariff relief.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested as much in a Monday interview, telling CNBC that both sides discussed lowering tariffs on “noncritical” items.

But there has been no public movement on the board of investment, which the White House said was intended to provide a forum to discuss “investment-related issues.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week during an interview with Fox News that China has made progress toward buying the 200 Boeing planes initially agreed upon, but no purchase has been announced. Trump has said the deal eventually was expected to be for 750 planes, though Greer did not mention anything about additional aircraft. The U.S. official said the deal had been on thin ice after disagreements between China and Boeing. The White House initially touted the agreement as a significant victory for the Trump administration because it had been years since China purchased Boeing planes.

Jamieson Greer AP-25099609540207 (7476x4984, AR: 1.50)
“There's a long history of teeing up ideas and possibilities and then sort of at the eleventh hour the Chinese will come in with some condition and crater it essentially,” said Russel. “It’s done for strategic reasons. It's the way they operate to try and keep everything all balanced and so they can, in part, test what the U.S. really wants.”

Concerning the agricultural agreement — the issue perhaps most closely aligned with the president’s domestic agenda — those tracking the purchases say China has made significant progress buying soybeans from American farmers. As of Sept. 11, the American Soybean Association estimates Chinese buyers have ordered 15.5 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans this season. China committed to buy at least 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans this marketing year.

But agricultural purchases outside of soybeans are lacking. Ishan Bhanu, the lead agricultural commodities analyst at the data firm Kpler, says other American products China would likely buy include corn, wheat, cotton and peanuts. Bhanu said those purchases have been slower to materialize, with only $3 billion bought so far — equating to roughly a half-billion per month.

“When we cut the data — call it pro-rated since May or since June — anyway we look at it, there has been no progress towards this commitment,” Bhanu said. Bhanu said corn is the only commodity that China buys in excess that would meet its commitments. But the large amount needed would send corn prices in both the U.S. and abroad skyrocketing, he said, creating an additional problem for the countries.

The fight over critical minerals and the supply chain remains the issue on which the U.S. and China have struggled to bridge their gap. Two sources say the Trump administration believes China has done the bare minimum to live up to the May agreement, which the document circulated by the White House said would also address U.S. concern about China blocking Americans from purchasing rare earth production equipment.

“No surprise,” the U.S. official said, adding that China doesn’t “live up to their commitments, ever.”

Schuman predicted that the lack of progress on addressing the critical mineral issue would factor into whether the U.S. extends the one-year “strategic stability” truce.

Ultimately, Xi’s visit is significant, though it’s expected to produce less-than-significant results. But any progress at all could be enough for the Trump administration to consider it a win, according to multiple people familiar with the relationship.

Ryan Hass, who served on the White House National Security Council from 2013 to 2017, said achieving small diplomatic gains would be a positive development, given the precarious dynamics between the world’s preeminent superpowers.

“I don’t think there will be any great surprises,” said Hass, who is now the director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. “President Trump is just preternaturally predisposed to highlight and tout the fact that China wants to buy American products.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Jury’s Out
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 23, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Closing arguments in the Trayon White trial, how D.C. government wants to use AI and the Mystics’ playoff push.

Capital Weather's Daily Digit: 4/10. Another cloudy, damp and cool day puts summer farther back in the rearview mirror on this first full day of fall. Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

The jury in the Trayon White trial is expected to begin deliberations today.

White, who maintains his innocence, stands accused of accepting cash bribes from a D.C. government contractor in exchange for agreeing to help him continue to secure lucrative city work in violence intervention.

The question for the jury is not whether White took the money, The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports. His defense does not deny that he did (and that’s seen clearly on tape!). Instead, the jury must decide a more complicated question: whether White intended to be influenced to act in ways that qualify as bribery under federal law.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Ross argued Tuesday that White clearly “sold his position, his power, his access for his own personal greed.”

The defense, however, said prosecutors had not done enough to prove that White acted or intended to act corruptly.

“There is no evidence Trayon White has done a corrupt thing, then or ever,” said Gary Kohlman, one of White’s attorneys, in his closing argument.

White opted not to testify, as is his right. But on Tuesday, he still logged into the D.C. Council’s meetings via Zoom — even chiming in at one point.

During a discussion about opioid-related services, White asked who currently had a contract with the D.C. government to do that work in Ward 8.

Then — never mind.

“I don’t want to talk about contractors right now,” he said with a laugh.


DEEP DIVE

Identifying vacant homes. Screening 911 and 311 calls for quality. Improving benefit payments.

These are just some of the ways D.C. government wants to use AI to stretch its limited resources, automate tedious paperwork and generally speed up city services, The Sun’s Zara Norman, Martin Austermuhle and Michael Brice-Saddler report.

In February 2024, Mayor Muriel Bowser established ground rules for how District agencies adopt AI, detailing six core values — including privacy, equity and human accountability — that they must weigh in doing so. The order also created a citywide AI task force, set a timeline requiring every agency to submit a formal strategic plan by October 2026, and gave the Office of the Chief Technology Officer broad authority to vet any new technology.

Now those ideas are in, and Chris Rodriguez, the assistant city administrator for OCTO, stressed that he doesn’t see AI substituting for city workers. “It’s meant to assist,” he said. “It’s not meant to replace.”

Still, concerns linger in a city with the highest unemployment rate in the country. Many residents worry about privacy, too. “One of the top concerns many parents have is, how is our kids’ data being used?” said Maya Mechenbier, a DCPS parent and leader of Schools Beyond Screens D.C.

Most residents who turned up to public AI task force hearings expressed “cautious optimism,” said Christopher Jordan, a program manager of AI and innovation at the National League of Cities. “When the public can see inside the city’s strategy and their intent, I think that it just creates a much better forum to have these conversations, rather than starting with distrust.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

D.C.’s ballot initiatives may soon face new restrictions. The D.C. Council has given initial approval to a bill that adds new regulations on the city’s ballot initiatives, which allow residents to bypass lawmakers and approve laws themselves. Proponents say the new rules are meant to give the public more chances to weigh in on proposed initiatives, while critics say they’re an underhanded attempt to kill them off.

D.C. had no local colleges crack the top 20 in the latest U.S. News and World Report listing of the nation’s best universities. Georgetown was ranked highest, tying at No. 23, and Howard made a historic 15-point leap up to No. 73. According to WTOP, both American University and the University of Maryland at College Park slid down in their rankings, in part due to a decline in Pell Grant enrollments.

Punk is back! Two fans are working to revive D.C.'s politically charged punk rock scene with a mutual aid concert this weekend on the National Mall, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports.

Going for gold. Metro is celebrating its golden anniversary by releasing five commemorative gold-tinted Smart Trip card designs to mark five decades of service. About 20,000 of each design will be available at “select stations” starting Thursday, with a new design rolled out every two weeks.

A D.C. judge has ordered a prominent developer to start improving housing conditions at a troubled building the developer owns in Northeast, City Cast D.C. reports. Conditions at the Delta Pearl drew the attention of D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb, who sued developer Buwa Binitie this month over what he called “extreme disrepair and neglect.” The situation attracted more attention last week when Binitie’s lawyer — a former D.C. attorney general — argued with building tenants at a protest.

Police say a cyclist was killed Tuesday in a collision with a truck near Logan Circle, ABC7 reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Officials with the Prince George’s County Police Department have ruled the death of a Black man found hanging on the side of a road in Upper Marlboro to be a suicide, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For theater lovers: Theatre Week, through Oct. 11.

For Eurovision fans: MARO at The Black Cat, Saturday.

For the folksy: Takoma Park Folk Festival, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

At this time a year ago, the Nationals were still in the process of hiring Paul Toboni, who officially started as president of baseball operations on Oct. 1, 2025. Once he was in the job, he turned over the entire operation at a breakneck pace, leading to dozens of new hires for the front office, major league coaching staff and player development system. With less than a week left in his first season on the job, that process is continuing. The Nats are reportedly hiring Brian Rodgers as their next director of international scouting, as The Sun’s Alex Schiffer writes. Rodgers had been with the Houston Astros since 2022.

The Mystics’ playoff fate is getting (a little) clearer. They handled business on Tuesday with a 79-69 win over the Connecticut Sun. (Shakira Austin put some finishing touches on her case for Most Improved Player with 25 points and 13 rebounds.) The Mystics’ playoff seeding will not be clear until the regular season wraps on Thursday, but the win last night seriously helps their chances of moving up the standings. If they can get one more win in their regular season finale Thursday against Chicago, they’ll have a real shot at the best possible outcome as the fifth seed.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Tigers, 1:10 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Nikie Johnson, Jeff Dooley and Jaden Amos.

entries.title: The Washington Sun: Skynet, Rebranded
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump’s toughest nickname challenge yet. What to expect from Xi Jinping’s state visit. A scoop about RFK Jr. and cancer screenings. A big shift for Republicans on the campaign trail. And: What’s going on in Montana?  





THE LATEST

How smart is Super Intelligence? Still a believer in unfettered artificial intelligence development, Donald Trump has a new phrase he plans to repeat to drown out the growing bipartisan backlash to the technology.

“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence — SI — let’s see if that goes. It sounds much better,” Trump said in his United Nations address. “The word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake.”

This president has a way with words more potent than most. Trump’s nicknames for his opponents and turns of phrases have changed political discourses before. “I’m sure it’s branding,” a former Trump official told our Ben T.N. Mause. “‘AI’ is toxic.”

But when it comes to SI, it may be wise to heed Inigo Montoya: You keep using that word. I do not think it means what you think it means.

This is an industry that absolutely needs someone to lead it to a kinder, gentler public perception. Active participants in the AI debate see more than a nomenclature problem. “Names certainly can matter — renaming the ‘estate tax’ the ‘death tax’ proved politically impactful,” veteran lobbyist Bruce Mehlman told us. “But shifting from AI to SI seems less likely to alleviate concerns over electricity costs, cyber risk or societal safety, especially in the next two months.”

Polling bears this out. Public faith in this tech is tanking, even as confusion about it remains high. “My sense is that adding a word in front of AI, whether it is general intelligence or super intelligence, isn’t a distinction that matters to the public,” Lee Rainie, an expert in public opinion around AI at Elon University, told us. “Experts cannot agree on what the definition of artificial general intelligence is or the definition of artificial super intelligence. Asking people to sort these differences out isn’t a very reasonable thing to do.”

Does super intelligence sound less scary … or more scary? This was the term used in some of the original books about what to fear from this technology. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) has used it to describe the most dangerous outcomes from AI development for a while now. In fact, he and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) invited reporters to a call today about the lawmakers’ efforts to legislatively corral what they call “superintelligence,” defined as “machines humans cannot control.”

More: Federal Lawmakers Score Major Paydays From Books • Appeals Court Rejects Post-9/11 Restrictions on Capitol Steps Protests • Trump Backs Ban on Diesel Exports Amid Growing Calls From Republicans

Open tabs:

  • Another U.S. service member dies amid Iran war, Pentagon tally shows (WaPo)
  • RFK Jr.’s Enhanced Security Was Funded With Money From Minority Health Office (WSJ)
  • Hospitals Shutter Youth Gender Clinics in Deal With Trump Administration (NYT)
  • What is in the US-Greenland-Denmark security deal? (Reuters)




FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


State visit: Expectations are not high for major diplomatic news from Chinese President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington starting today, The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright and Ben T.N. Mause report. The visit is expected to be big on diplomatic pomp, however, as it is Xi’s first official state visit since 2015. “I think the status quo with China is not great by any stretch, but it’s better than the alternative: a tariff war and a limited supply of our rare critical minerals,” said one U.S. official. “So I think that the expectation is it’s mostly going to be kicking the can.”

FROM THE HILL


First on The Sun: Mitch McConnell presses Trump on Taiwan. The Republican senator from Kentucky is leading an effort to make sure Xi’s visit does not lead the White House to offer any concessions over Taiwan, our Joe Gould reports. A letter from McConnell and other Republicans who are sometimes thorns in Trump’s side — Sens. John Cornyn of Texas, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — demands that the Trump administration get moving on more than $1 billion in direct military aid already authorized and a $14 billion arms deal for the island. “We are concerned by President Trump’s description of Taiwan as ‘a very good negotiating chip,’” the letter reads.

FROM HHS


Scoop: RFK Jr. privately backs controversial cancer-screening tests. In a private meeting last winter, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said he’d like the Preventive Services Task Force to recommend multi-cancer blood tests, sources tell The Sun’s Paige Winfield Cunningham. The tests can detect early-stage cancer when it’s more treatable but can also give false alarms that push patients toward additional interventions they wouldn’t have otherwise sought. Leading medical associations don’t recommend for or against them for people without symptoms, Paige writes.

Four companies that make or sell early-detection cancer tests or scans are involved in the Make America Healthy Again Summit next week, including as corporate sponsors.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


That thing that was not supposed to happen has happened. Trump’s iron grip on Republican electeds really has slipped, The Sun’s Igor Bobic reports. In the past week, a Republican congresswoman denounced Trump’s immigration policies, a Republican senator called for a probe into his son’s wedding and two Republican Senate candidates urged him to swiftly end the Iran war.

The law of political gravity, it seems, still applies. But that doesn’t mean it’s going to change those midterm polls. “Unless it has been part of your brand for some time, I’m not sure voters will really buy it,” a longtime Republican strategist said.





PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: On this week’s Washington Sun Cast, Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) gave The Sun’s Kadia Goba a stern “no” when asked if he was confident Democrats will win the House majority — though he was “confident we will put forth our best effort.” The party will win, he says, if everybody “really goes to work.” The longtime congressman also talked about his role in keeping South Carolina as the first Democratic primary state for 2028 and what makes a good fish fry.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Is Sam Forstag the next Montana Democrat? The state has had its share of national party figures, but is generally seen as a conservative, small-government bastion. The Sun’s Anna Kramer traveled to the western part of this vast state to trail Forstag, a former Forest Service smokejumper and local union leader turned congressional candidate, who is making the case that Trump’s particular version of small government is not the right fit for Montana.

DOGE cuts and Trump’s public land policies have left their mark on a state that relies on the federal workforce: “The current administration is screwing up so badly that it’s really creating an opening,” a retired Republican state lawmaker told Anna.

But Forstag is also asking a lot of this electorate. The Cook Political Report rates the seat as “likely R,” and Forstag is running with the unabashed endorsement of Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), two names Republicans are thrilled to run against. Is the next Montana Democrat that kind of Democrat? Anna goes deep in her story.

entries.title: McConnell Leads Republicans in Demanding Trump Release Funding and Weapons to Taiwan
entries.summary: The request comes as fears grow that the president will make concessions to China on the island’s security.
entries.content:
Republicans led by Sen. Mitch McConnell are pressing the Trump administration to release $1.3 billion in military aid to Taiwan and approve a stalled $14 billion arms package, as fears grow that President Donald Trump will make concessions on Taiwan security when he meets this week with Xi Jinping.

The letter, sent Wednesday by McConnell and three other senators, comes as the Chinese leader is expected to press Trump to curb U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and concerns grow in Washington that the president could use security assistance for the island as leverage in negotiations with Beijing. The letter, shared with The Washington Sun, and the delay in sending the aid money to Taiwan had not been previously reported.

The senators, in the letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, questioned why the State Department has not obligated $300 million in foreign military financing that Congress provided for Taiwan in the fiscal 2026 budget and why the Pentagon has not obligated another $1 billion that Congress provided through the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, a program to bolster the island’s defenses. The lawmakers also challenge the administration’s freeze on $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan.

“We are concerned by President Trump’s description of Taiwan as ‘a very good negotiating chip’ in engagements with Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party,” the senators wrote. “It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities.”

Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina signed the letter.

Congress has long played a central role in U.S. support for Taiwan, particularly through the Taiwan Relations Act, a 1979 law that committed the U.S. to making defensive weapons and services available to Taiwan after Washington formally switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China.

China hawks are now urging Trump not to let economic concerns overshadow security. Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), in a floor speech Tuesday that criticized Trump’s lavish reception for Xi, called on the president to confront Xi over Taiwan and China’s military coercion of its neighbors.

“I know the president tends to discuss trade and artificial intelligence with the Chinese leadership, and rightfully so; perhaps some progress will be made,” Wicker said. “But during every minute of dialogue, our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors, and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”

Wicker said after leaving the Senate floor that he is “very much in favor” of the administration moving forward with the $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan and formally notifying Congress of its intention to do so.

The dispute between members of Congress and the White House lands at a sensitive moment in Trump’s relationship with China. Taiwan was a major point of contention at Trump and Xi’s last meeting in May, when Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could lead to conflict.

Xi is expected to use his White House meeting with Trump on Thursday to push for limits on U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan, Reuters reported this week. Beijing has long opposed American military support for the self-governed island, which China claims as its territory.

At the same time, the Trump administration is prioritizing Chinese investment in the United States, cooperation on artificial intelligence and continued access to critical minerals and rare earths from China that are essential to U.S. commercial and defense manufacturing.

That has raised questions in Taiwan and among its supporters in Washington about whether Trump could hold back security assistance to the island as part of a broader compromise with Beijing.

Michael Pillsbury, who has advised Trump on China, said senior Chinese officials have told him that their top goal for the talks is a U.S. concession on Taiwan independence. But he said they recognize that this is a shift the administration is unlikely to make.

Pillsbury said the officials nevertheless see Trump as more flexible on Taiwan than former President Joe Biden.

“Taiwan leadership is quite worried,” Pillsbury said. “Biden four times said words to the effect of, ‘We have to defend Taiwan.’ … Mr. Trump has not ever said, ‘We have to defend Taiwan.’ They have almost a sense of suspicion that this is too good to be true.”

Trump has said he is open to using the arms package as leverage. In an interview with Fox News after traveling to China in May to meet with Xi, Trump said he was holding the major weapons package for Taiwan “in abeyance,” calling it “a very good negotiating chip for us.”

Foreign military financing provides U.S. grants and loans that international partners can use to buy American-made defense equipment, services and training. In February, Trump signed the consolidated spending bill for 2026, in which Congress directed that at least $300 million be made available for Taiwan.

According to a White House Office of Management and Budget database, Jordan, Israel, Thailand and the Philippines have already received approval for funds from the 2026 foreign military financing budget, while Taiwan was not listed among the recipients.

The administration has missed the deadline for moving the money under the normal process. The funds expire Sept. 30, and the State Department would have had to notify Congress by Sept. 15 to obligate them before then, according to a congressional aide who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions.

Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, told The Sun that the Taiwan money is part of a wider freeze affecting new U.S. security assistance and arms-sale notifications for Taiwan.

The administration last approved arms sales for Taiwan in December: a $11 billion package, which was the largest by dollar value. There’s been a backlog of proposed sales since then, including Patriot Advanced Capability-3 and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System air defenses.

Delaying or canceling those sales would also complicate another Trump administration goal, according to Hammond-Chambers. Taipei has said that without substantial new purchases of American weapons, it will struggle to increase defense spending to 5% of its gross domestic product by 2030, as Trump has insisted.

“The Taiwan government is pointing out: Look, we budgeted this stuff on the back of your assurance that the sales will be processed this year,” Hammond-Chambers said. “In Taiwan, if budgeted money does not get spent by the end of the year, it goes back to their treasury, right? It's lost money.”

entries.title: Federal Lawmakers Score Major Paydays From Books
entries.summary: Some lawmakers’ book sales have exceeded their paychecks from Congress.
entries.content:
Members of Congress haven’t received a raise in nearly two decades, and federal law severely restricts them from working side gigs to pad their personal finances.

But at least nine federal lawmakers waltzed through a literary loophole last year, earning income from book writing last year that rivaled — and in four instances, exceeded — their $174,000-per-year congressional salaries, according to a Washington Sun analysis of House and Senate financial disclosures.

A couple dozen others earned four- or five-figure paydays in 2025 or are actively writing books that could score them handsome amounts of supplementary cash.

These days, book-writing is all but perfunctory for Capitol Hill’s leadership aspirants and potential presidential candidates. Political committees, meanwhile, have recently juiced sales by spending five- or six-figure amounts on bulk book orders of their allies’ tomes and treatises, according to Federal Election Commission records. Here’s a complete rundown of who in Congress — along with a couple of prominent congressional hopefuls — is scoring the most money:


Six-Figure Club


Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey)

The evening of March 31, 2025, Booker stood up on the Senate floor and began speaking. It’d be another 25 hours and five minutes before he stood down and concluded his remarks. A year later, Booker’s appropriately titled book, “Stand,” hit bookstores as a meditation on civic virtues and responsibilities.

It’s also a lesson in capitalism: The potential 2028 presidential hopeful last year scored $365,000 — more than twice his Senate salary — in the form of a book advance from St. Martin’s Publishing Group. Booker embarked on a nine-city book tour in March and April.

“Cory’s team worked closely with the Senate Ethics Committee and legal counsel to follow all ethical and legal guidelines relating to his book,” spokesperson David Bergstein said in a statement.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania)

Fetterman last year earned $345,000 for his 2025 book “Unfettered,” published by Penguin Random House. That’s on top of the $172,500 he earned from the book in 2024, the year he signed a royalty agreement. The senator’s 240-page memoir explores Fetterman’s path to power, life-altering stroke, mental health struggles and contrarian politics that have alienated many of his fellow Democrats.

The book was hardly a commercial blockbuster, failing to land on major nonfiction bestseller lists despite the uncredited involvement of Pulitzer Prize-winning author Buzz Bissinger of “Friday Night Lights” fame. Defector writer Alex Shultz reported in November that the Barnes & Noble of Fetterman’s hometown of York, Pennsylvania, didn’t sell a single copy of “Unfettered” in the two days after its release. Fetterman’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont)

US politician Bernie Sanders presents book (7094x4729, AR: 1.50)
Books are a significant reason for Sanders’ increase in wealth to millionaire status — or close. In 2025, he earned $200,000 in royalties from Penguin Random House as his latest book, “Fight Oligarchy,” hit bookstores and became a New York Times bestseller. In 2024, Sanders earned $148,750 from Penguin Random House, which also published his previous book, “It’s OK to Be Angry About Capitalism.” Sanders’ office did not respond to requests for comment.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas)

One of Capitol Hill’s most prolific authors, Cotton has written three books since 2019, including his most recent, “Seven Things You Can’t Say About China.” He is under contract to write two more: “Seven Things You Can't Say About the Left” and a yet-to-be-titled sequel. Last year, the senator earned $190,032 in royalties across several book revenue streams — mostly from Harper Collins Publishing, but also foreign publishers in Japan, Poland, Estonia and South Korea. Cotton maintains a limited liability company, TBC Books LLC, to manage his authorly pursuits. Cotton’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas)

During 2025, Cruz made $155,312 from a book advance through Penguin Random House, which published his August 2026 book, “Going Further: The Incomparable Clarence Thomas,” about the Supreme Court justice. But this only represents a fraction of Cruz’s recent literary haul. Since 2020, Cruz has booked more than $2.32 million in advances, according to a financial filing he submitted to the Senate on Aug. 13. In the past, Cruz’s own campaign committee has been a prime customer for his books. Cruz, who placed a distant second to President Donald Trump in the 2016 contest, is actively considering running for president in 2028.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Cruz’s Senate office said the senator has written five New York Times bestsellers. “The income referenced in his financial disclosure reflects an advance for his writing,” the statement said. “Actual royalties beyond the advance are donated to charity. Senator Cruz is an avid writer and enjoys storytelling, particularly as a way to take readers behind the scenes of consequential moments and figures through his unique lens."

Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York)

The Senate minority leader’s 2025 book, “Antisemitism in America: A Warning,” earned Schumer a $100,001 payout last year through a limited liability company — NEH 3 LLC — that the senator “established to receive income” from the book’s publication. Schumer also reported that his wife received a separate $100,001 payment through the LLC. The book became a bestseller. Schumer’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona)

The potential 2028 presidential candidate made $100,000 last year from an advance stemming from his 2025 royalty agreement with Simon & Schuster LLC for a yet-to-be-released book Gallego says is titled “American Corrido.” Gallego lists his “net” income from the advance as $51,000 — what his office says is the amount he earned after paying a co-author and taxes.

“Senator Gallego’s story is a uniquely American one. He was raised by a single mother, served in the Marines in Iraq, worked his way through Harvard, and became a United States senator,” spokesperson Jacques Petit said. “He looks forward to sharing his story with readers.”

Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California)

Nancy Pelosi (6000x3994, AR: 1.50)
The House speaker emeritus’ 2024 book, “The Art of Power,” published by Simon & Schuster, scored her between $100,001 and $1 million in 2025. (Unlike in the Senate, House members are only required to list book-related income in broad ranges.) Pelosi’s book debuted in late August 2024 as No. 1 on the New York Times bestseller list for hardcover nonfiction. Pelosi’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky)

Comer owns a limited liability company, Gamaliel Stargazer LLC, that “was formed to own any future royalties from upcoming book sales” from “All The President’s Money” — a scathing assessment, published in 2025, of former President Joe Biden. In his annual personal financial disclosure, Comer doesn’t specify how much he earned last year from his book. Instead, he states that Gamaliel Stargazer LLC earned between $100,000 and $1 million during 2025. Comer’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Five-Figure Club


Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina)

The also-ran 2024 presidential candidate scored a $94,563 in royalties last year from HarperCollins, which published his 2025 book, “One Nation Always Under God: Profiles in Christian Courage,” and his 2022 book, “America, a Redemption Story.”

Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana)

U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)
“How to Test Negative for Stupid: And Why Washington Never Will” — Kennedy’s romp through the absurdities and goofiness of political life on Capitol Hill — landed him an extended and improbable trip to the bestseller list after it published in October 2025. It also made the folksy senator $91,562 in the form of a book advance last year from HarperCollins Publishers.

Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia)

Warnock disclosed $66,256 in book-related earnings during 2025, mostly from Penguin Random House, including for his most recent effort, “The Crooked Places Made Straight.” Income also includes about $500 he made last year from his 2014 book, “The Divided Mind of the Black Church: Theology, Piety, and Public Witness,” published through New York University Press.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona)

A potential presidential candidate, Kelly signed an agreement last year with Simon & Schuster to “receive book advance and royalty payments” for a yet-to-be published book titled “Dr. Atticus Orbit's Guide to Becoming an Astronaut.’ Kelly, a retired astronaut, has previously penned children’s books including “Mousetronaut Saves the World” and “Astrotwins — Project Blastoff.” He reported receiving $51,928 total in 2025 from book-connected money.

Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri)

Schmitt reported receiving a “partial advance payment” of $41,667 in 2025 for his bestselling book “The Last Line of Defense: How to Beat the Left in Court,” which published last year.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts)

The author of more than a dozen books, Warren’s oldest writings — academic books dating to the 1980s and 1990s — are the ones generating cash, according to her 2025 financial disclosure, which indicated she earned $23,178.

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pennsylvania)

McCormick made $20,180 from “book proceeds” last year. He co-wrote the 2025 book “Who Believed in You: How Purposeful Mentorship Changes the World,” with his wife, Dina Powell McCormick, and the 2023 title “Superpower in Peril: A Battle Plan to Renew America” with adviser James M. Cunningham.

Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska)

Murkowski pocketed $14,750 in 2025 for her book “Far From Home,” which published last year.

Abdul El-Sayed

The Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan has three book royalty agreements dating to last decade. He disclosed that royalties from his books are paid to a AME Higher LLC, a company he owns. El-Sayed reported receiving a $103,000 payout in 2025 from AME Higher LLC, although it’s unclear how much of that is derived from book income. El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to questions about how much money he received.



Clearance Sale

Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Montana)

Sheehy earned $6,541 last year from his 2023 book “Mudslingers: A True Story of Aerial Firefighting.” But he says he didn’t keep the money: “Royalties donated to charity,” his financial disclosure affirmed. Business Insider also reported that Sheehy planned to donate some of his book money to a Washington, D.C.-based lobbying group he helped found. The book garnered some controversy: The Daily Montanan and Montana Public Radio reported that it included passages from other sources without crediting them. Sheehy did not comment on the reports at the time and didn’t return a request for comment.

Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio)

Jordan’s book “Do What You Said You Would Do” is now five years old, but it still earned the House Judiciary Committee chairman between $2,501 and $5,000 in royalties. Another Jordan book from more than 30 years ago, “Victory at the Training Table: A Guide to Sports Nutrition,” also earned him up to $200.

Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kansas)

Davids reported earning royalties of between $2,501 and $5,000 related to her 2021 illustrated children’s book “Sharice’s Big Voice.”

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky)

Paul may have six active book royalty agreements dating to the early 2010s. But he only reported $1,000 in book income during 2025, all coming from his 2023 book, “Deception: The Great Covid Cover-Up.”

Free Table


Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tennessee)

Blackburn, who’s running for Tennessee governor, reported no income in 2025 from her 2020 children’s book, “Camilla Can Vote,” which she wrote with her adult daughter and distributed through conservative publishing house Brave Books LLC.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota)

Amy Klobuchar (2100x1416, AR: 1.48)
Klobuchar, who’s running for Minnesota governor, wrote her first book in the mid-1980s and three since, including a 2023 memoir, “The Joy of Politics: Surviving Cancer, a Campaign, a Pandemic, an Insurrection, and Life’s Other Unexpected Curveballs.” Klobuchar reported receiving no royalty money for any of them during 2025.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-California)

Book money appears to have dried up for the freshman senator, as Schiff reported no income in 2025 from “Midnight in Washington: How We Almost Lost Our Democracy and Still Could,” which published in 2021 and earned $8,339 in 2024.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri)

None of the three books that Hawley has written this decade — including his most recent from 2023, “Manhood: The Masculine Virtues America Needs” — generated income for him during 2025.

Sen. Katie Britt (R-Alabama)

Britt’s 2023 memoir/self-help book, “God Calls Us to Do Hard Things: Lessons From the Alabama Wiregrass,” did not earn her royalties in 2025 from publisher Hachette Book Group.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Virginia)

Kaine’s 2024 memoir “Walk Ride Paddle” didn’t generate a penny in royalties from publisher Harper Horizon.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island)

Whitehouse acknowledged that “no royalties were received in 2025” from any of the three books he’s written during the past 13 years, including his most recent, 2022’s “The Scheme.”

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa)

Ernst’s 2020 book, “Daughter of the Heartland: My Ode to the Country That Raised Me,” paid her no residuals in 2025.

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon)

Neither Merkley’s 2019 “America is Better Than This” nor his 2023 “Filibustered!” earned him income in 2025 despite ongoing royalty agreements with his publishers.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)

Duckworth’s 2021 book, “Every Day is a Gift: A Memoir,” had no income attached last year although she retains a royalty agreement with the Hachette Book Group.

Newer Arrivals


Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina)

“How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents” is the title of an upcoming book for Tillis, who’s embraced his status as an outcast within his own party. The outgoing senator, who did not seek reelection amid constant sparring with Trump, signed a publishing contract with HarperCollins earlier this year, which Tillis says “provides for royalty payments, including an advance on royalty payments.” Terms have not yet been disclosed.

Sen. John Thune (R-South Dakota)

The Senate majority leader inked a deal in February with Hachette Book Group for a “forthcoming but untitled book” that comes with “an advance of royalties.” Thune affirmed he had not yet received any money from it entering 2026.

Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah)

Lee’s latest book, “The UniParty,” published this summer, after he signed a deal — terms undisclosed — with HarperCollins Publishers in late 2024. Lee reported earning no advance money related to this book during 2025. He also reported no income last year from any of several other books he’s written during the past 15 years.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut)

In February 2026, Murphy reached an “advance and royalties” agreement with publisher Farrar Straus Giroux for “Crisis of the Common Good,” which published in May. Murphy did not disclose terms in his most recent financial disclosure, which covered activity during calendar year 2025.

James Talarico

The Senate candidate is hoping to become the first Democrat elected to statewide office in Texas since President Bill Clinton’s first term. If so, that’ll likely help sales of Talarico’s “untitled” future book published by HarperCollins Publishers LLC, with which he signed an advance and royalties agreement in March. Talarico did not disclose terms.

entries.title: Kennedy Privately Backs Cancer-Detection Tests With Ties to MAHA
entries.summary: Several key industry players developing the tests are sponsoring or speaking at the Make America Healthy Again Summit next week, which will be attended by top health officials.
entries.content:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. privately said he wants the federal government to recommend a cancer-detection test that has sharply divided medical professionals but has close financial ties to the Make America Healthy Again movement.

Those ties could prove influential in the coming weeks as Kennedy moves to reshape preventative health care, and crucial votes Wednesday at the Food and Drug Administration stand to determine the future of this industry.

In a private meeting last winter to discuss overhauling a panel of advisers that determines essential preventive services, Kennedy said he’d like it to recommend multi-cancer blood tests, according to a former Health and Human Services official who was in the meeting.

The meeting included Kennedy’s senior counselor Stefanie Spear; chief policy counselor Ken Callahan; Mitchell Hailstone, a former director of public strategy; and Roger Klein, director of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

Another former HHS official said he repeatedly heard Kennedy say he’d like the task force to recommend the tests.

Those tests are controversial in preventive health. They can detect early-stage cancer when it’s more treatable but can also give false alarms that push patients toward additional interventions they wouldn’t have otherwise sought. Leading medical associations don’t recommend for or against them for people without symptoms.

But the industry has deep ties to MAHA and has Kennedy’s ear. Makers of those cancer-screening tests and scans are sponsoring next week’s Make America Healthy Again Summit, paying to mingle with top Trump administration health officials as they petition the federal government to endorse their products.

Four companies that make or sell early-detection cancer tests or scans are involved in the one-day, corporate-sponsored summit, where health industry leaders and administration officials will share the stage at the Waldorf Astoria to discuss longevity, prevention and other hot topics in the MAHA movement Kennedy leads.

Biotech company Grail, whose multi-cancer blood test Galleri is up for a FDA vote Wednesday, and Prenuvo, which sells a full-body MRI scan, are among the summit’s sponsors. Grail CEO Joshua Ofman and Superpower CEO Max Marchione, whose company sells Galleri, are slated to speak on panels.

So is longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, who helped design another full-body scan sold by Ezra, a company acquired by Function Health, which is led by Kennedy’s friend Mark Hyman.

Galleri uses blood from a single draw to screen for a DNA signal shared by more than 50 cancer types. Superpower sells it for $949. Prenuvo sells its whole-body scan for around $2,500.

Companies making and selling these tests have been seeking buy-in from the experts whose recommendations guide millions of Americans on when and how to get screened for cancer.

“Screening is much more complicated than just ‘Do the test and if you find something it’s wonderful,’” said Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University who has consulted for Grail.

One of those groups the industry is looking for approval from is the Preventive Services Task Force, a panel of outside advisers whose recommendations determine which screening tests private insurers must cover for free.

Kennedy, who has previously called the task force “lackadaisical,” named eight new members last week as part of an effort to reshape the body. He hasn’t publicly said how he wants the task force to operate. But, in a departure from the norm of filling it with primary-care doctors, he did appoint specialists to the panel, among them a radiologist.

The group hasn’t issued a recommendation for or against diagnostics like the ones sold by Grail and Prenuvo.

Prenuvo’s chief medical officer, Dan Durand, said “it’s fantastic” to have a radiologist on the task force. But Durand insisted his company isn’t seeking reimbursement for its full-body MRI by sponsoring the MAHA Summit.

“That is not what we’re looking for,” Durand told The Washington Sun. “We’re looking to be understood, we’re looking to contribute to the conversation about ending the chronic-disease epidemic.”

Neither Grail nor Prenuvo would say how much they paid for their sponsorships. Superpower, Hyman and HHS did not respond to a request for comment.

Asked about Grail’s participation in the summit, Ofman told The Sun, “We welcome the opportunity to participate in any forum that discusses health policy to improve the health of Americans through transitioning from a broken system to one focused on prevention and early detection.”

Earlier this year, summit organizer MAHA Action highlighted how a full-body scan detected early-stage lung cancer in Shira Boehler, the wife of Trump administration official and summit panelist Adam Boehler.

Grail is currently lobbying the FDA to approve Galleri, which would be the first approved multi-cancer early-detection test on the U.S. market. An advisory panel is scheduled to vote Wednesday on whether to recommend the agency grant approval.

Congress has already cleared a pathway for these tests. In February, President Donald Trump signed a law allowing Medicare to start paying for FDA-approved versions starting in 2028.

entries.title: Punk Rock Returns to the National Mall for the First Time in 30 Years
entries.summary: A Sept. 26 mutual aid benefit at the Sylvan Theater aims to revive the D.C.’s politically charged punk tradition.
entries.content:
More than 30 years after Fugazi played landmark shows at the Sylvan Theater on the National Mall, two punk fans are working to revive D.C.'s politically charged punk scene with a mutual aid concert this weekend.

For one of the show’s organizers, Caroline Liaupsin, the show is about more than bringing punk back to a historic stage. It is an attempt to remind fans of D.C.’s outspoken punk legacy as residents deal with rising costs, gentrification and loss of venues.

“Right now D.C. is maybe at its worst spot it’s been at in a very long time,” Liaupsin said, pointing to the presence of National Guard troops and Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

“The city is being treated like an experiment, basically, and not respected in the way that it should be, as a place where hundreds of thousands of people live and love and make art and want to have a city that is theirs,” she said.

That sense of political urgency has long been part of the District’s punk identity.

“What made D.C.’s punks unique was the very explicitly political bent that they always had,” Liaupsin said, citing the legacy of bands and activist organizations that include Fugazi, Minor Threat, Revolution Summer and Positive Force D.C.

“Being a punk in D.C. sort of requires you to have an eye towards national politics in a way that you might not have to in other scenes across the country,” she said. “Because it’s all right there.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The Sylvan Theater is central to that history. Fugazi played there in 1993 and 1995, shows that Liaupsin said represented some of the band’s largest crowds and remain influential, with recordings of the performances still available online.

Saturday’s concert will feature Glitterer, Posición Unida and Somebody’s Daughter. Liaupsin expects more than 1,000 people to attend.

The idea for the new show began in January, when Liaupsin interviewed Glitterer’s Ned Russin for her radio program, DIYNot. During a break, Russin asked whether it might be possible to put on a show at the Sylvan.

At the time, Liaupsin thought it was impossible. But she had previously worked as a National Park Service ranger on the Mall and started working with people in the agency’s permitting office to see whether it could happen.

The event will also reflect changes in the District’s current music community. Liaupsin said the lineup was intentionally built to include representation for Latino and transgender people, pointing to Posición Unida’s Spanish-language hardcore and the fact that all of the members of Somebody’s Daughter identify as transgender.

Liaupsin and her co-organizer, Eleanor Pampalone, are both trans women. She said transgender people are an important part of D.C.’s communities, making that visibility particularly significant amid what she described as a hostile national political environment.

“It feels really, really important to make it very publicly known that trans people are here in large numbers in D.C. and make this city move,” she said.

The show’s proceeds will go to Ward One Mutual Aid, after organizers cover expenses.

Organizing the concert has been difficult. Because the theater is on federal parkland, organizers cannot sell tickets or conventional band merchandise and must cover extensive permitting, insurance and production requirements themselves. People who want to attend can RSVP, but admission is free.

Liaupsin said those hurdles are part of why similar shows have been difficult to stage there over the past 30 years.

“It’s in some ways very impractical to do,” she said. “It requires a lot of legwork and a lot of people coming together to make this happen. But despite how impractical it is and how difficult it is, it’s worth it.”

The result is the first punk show at the theater in more than three decades.

“This is a show that has the potential to go down the annals of D.C. punk history in the same way that those Fugazi shows in the ’90s did,” Liaupsin said.

entries.title: D.C. Council Moves to Put New Limits on Ballot Initiatives
entries.summary: Lawmakers say ballot initiatives are out of control, while critics say the council is stifling public input.
entries.content:
The D.C. Council on Tuesday gave initial approval to a bill that would put new restrictions on ballot initiatives, raising concerns from critics that lawmakers are trying to kill off the city’s only tool that lets voters bypass the council and directly pass laws themselves.

The bill — authored by At-Large council member Anita Bonds — emerged from growing frustration among some lawmakers and business groups that progressive advocates have increasingly leveraged D.C.’s ballot initiative process to set drug policy, establish new minimum wages for restaurant workers and change how the city conducts elections.

D.C. joins two-dozen states in allowing some type of citizen ballot initiative — something it has done for almost 50 years. Under current law, any resident or group can propose an initiative; if they collect signatures from 5% of the city’s voters, it gets placed on the ballot. Initiatives cannot violate the U.S. Constitution or the city’s human rights law, directly appropriate money or impose taxes.

The marquee change in Bonds’ bill would limit any initiative to a single subject, a direct response to Initiative 83, which D.C. voters overwhelmingly approved in November 2024. It required D.C. to implement ranked-choice voting — first used in the June 2026 primary — and conduct semi-open primaries, which are set to start in 2028.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“People were confused,” Bonds told The Washington Sun, recounting that she got complaints from residents who supported either ranked-choice voting or semi-open primaries — but didn’t have the ability to vote for one or the other.

The bill would also slow the process from when an initiative is proposed to when its proponents can start collecting signatures to get it on the ballot. That, she said, would give the public more chances to weigh in with concerns.

“When the council proposes legislation, there are many steps that must take place,” she said. “These measures offer the community the opportunity to understand legislation. The initiative does not allow that process. The public is presented with an idea, we all go and we vote, and so therefore the subject is never given the time and attention that you get through the legislative process.”

In a nine-page letter sent to lawmakers last week, former D.C. Board of Elections Chair Gary Thompson criticized Bonds’ bill, saying it aimed to “strangle” ballot initiatives. Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker expressed similar reservations before voting against the bill.

“What we’re doing here is putting up many more barriers and steps and extending the timelines,” he said. “We’re making it harder for the public to engage in [the initiative] process.”

Lisa Rice, the co-founder of Grow Democracy D.C. and one of the main proponents of Initiative 83, was disappointed with the council’s vote, tying it to moves across the country to limit public engagement in government.

“It’s a really disturbing trend,” she told The Sun. “Because politicians don’t like what the voters are able to bring to the ballot, they want to destroy the process. The solution isn’t to firebomb the process.”

Still, some lawmakers said Bonds’ bill missed the broader challenges with the city’s initiative process — and what they said should be done to change it.

“We chose to have a representative democracy, not a direct democracy, for a reason. The bill doesn’t address what I see as their real issue: That a $25 minimum wage issue or rent freeze is something many voters might agree with but would have an impact on our city and economy,” said At-Large council member Elissa Silverman, calling the initiatives an “end run around the 13 of us.”

Silverman was referring to two ballot initiatives that are currently going through the process. One would increase D.C.’s minimum wage to $25 by 2029 and later phase out the tipped wage paid to restaurant workers. (D.C. voters have weighed in on the tipped wage twice before, and the council has repealed those measures in full or in part.) Another would impose a two-year rent freeze and create new rules for how D.C. spends money on affordable housing. Both could be on the ballot in 2027, if proponents collect the required number of signatures.

This November, D.C. voters will weigh in on a ballot initiative that seeks to ban the sale of foie gras.

Silverman said she’d rather D.C. follow the lead of states like Massachusetts and Michigan, which have indirect ballot initiatives. Under those systems, residents or groups can petition their lawmakers to take on a particular topic. If the council doesn’t, the issue is put to a public vote.

Silverman ultimately voted against Bonds’ bill, while Ward 4 council member and Democratic nominee for mayor, Janeese Lewis George, voted present. A final vote on the bill is expected in early October.
