entries.title: DOGE Upended His Work. Does Montana Care Enough to Vote for Him?
entries.summary: Democrat Sam Forstag was a smokejumper with the Forest Service when Trump took a sledgehammer to the federal workforce.
entries.content:
WESTERN MONTANA — The bartender at Beaverhead Brewing Company was arguing with one of his customers.

“You want to put me out of a job?” he said, pulling a pint and looking over his shoulder.

“You work for the federal government? Then yeah,” said the man sitting at the bar in Dillon, Montana, on the night before Labor Day.

The bartender’s day job is for the federal government; he is a range technician for the Bureau of Land Management. The patron is a local landowner. Neither man sees themselves as political, they told The Washington Sun. The upcoming election for outgoing Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke’s congressional seat wasn’t on their radar, either.

But that night they were disagreeing passionately about one of the issues defining the race to represent Western Montana: What value do federal workers bring for the people of Montana? Who should be responsible for caring for the state’s abundant public lands?

Sam Forstag, a 32-year-old Democrat, is running for Congress in Montana on the notion that he can turn that fervor into votes.

Before this campaign, Forstag was a member of an elite crew of Forest Service wildland firefighters in Montana called smokejumpers. He parachuted out of planes into the wilderness to try to stop wildfires well before they reached communities. For Western Montanans haunted annually by the spectre of devastating fire, it’s a job everyone understands.

When President Donald Trump and Elon Musk made an aggressive push to put federal workers out of their jobs in early 2025, Forstag, who had just won a union leadership position at the Forest Service, became a face of resistance against Musk’s DOGE. Then he decided he wanted to try and find his way to Washington, D.C., himself.

“Right at the end of the fire season, I looked around. It felt so obvious,” he said of deciding to run for office. “Wouldn’t you rather in three years look back and say, ‘I did everything I could?’”

Forstag’s decision to run, the unlikely coalition now forming around his campaign, and increasing voter frustration in the state are all products of the last year-and-a-half of choices made in Washington. Trump’s administration has reshaped public lands, withheld disaster aid and taken a sledgehammer to the federal workforce. In a district that overwhelmingly voted for the president, and where the Democrat is inextricably opposed to Trump, Forstag's candidacy is a clear test of those actions.

“The current administration is screwing up so badly that it's really creating an opening,” said Brian Putnam, a Republican who served in the Montana Legislature until 2023.

How big an opening depends on what frustrated Montanans like the two men at Beaverhead Brewing decide to do in November.

***

Forstag was in Maryland for union steward training when the Trump administration sent millions of federal workers an email encouraging them to voluntarily quit their government jobs. Within a month, the administration abruptly fired all its employees classified as "probationary," including hundreds of Forest Service workers in Montana.

Forstag and others scrambled. They gave their union members — and even those outside the union — guidance of what to do if they were fired. "He never excluded anybody," said former Montana Forest Service soil scientist Melissa Pingree, who worked with Forstag on the union.

It was around that time when Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) came to Montana as part of their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour. They asked the Forest Service union local if someone could speak about the impact of DOGE. Forstag volunteered and delivered a speech that changed the course of his career.

“We have hundreds of members who are out of work right now, and it is harder than it should be just to get information about that to ourselves, let alone to get it out to the public,” he told The Sun. “So, I decided to give that speech and get it out to the public.”
IMG_3405 copy.jpg (6110x4032, AR: 1.52)Thousands of people attended the rally. Videos of Forstag’s speech went viral. So viral that he was told that the higher-ups at the United States Department of Agriculture wanted him investigated and fired.

In the end, he was never fired. “If they are worried about the media blowback of a smokejumper giving a public speech about cuts to our public lands to public employees, the blowback's going to be a lot worse if they fire that smokejumper,” he said.

But in the time between Forstag’s first encounter with DOGE in January 2025 and today, hundreds of longtime Forest Service employees in Montana have quit or taken early retirement.

Those still left inside the agency are stretched thin, handling multiple jobs and under increasing scrutiny to justify their work, said one current federal worker in Western Montana. Several federal workers told The Sun that they are increasingly concerned about the fact that the Trump administration is now conducting a full-scale reorganization of the Forest Service.

Forstag is betting that the blowback can help secure him an unlikely victory.

***

The fundamentals of Montana politics are working heavily against Forstag. Jon Tester, the last Democrat to win statewide, lost his Senate reelection campaign in 2024 by just over seven points. That year, Zinke, who served as Interior secretary under Trump’s first administration before resigning amid multiple ethics inquiries, won the House seat Forstag is running for by nearly eight points.

Forstag’s Republican opponent, Aaron Flint, is a Trump-endorsed, longtime conservative radio show host who is widely seen as the clear front-runner. The Cook Political Report rates the race as “likely Republican.” The region’s liberal enclaves around Bozeman and Missoula are becoming increasingly conservative, and aren’t populous enough to carry the district.

IMG_3348 (1) copy.jpg (3024x2016, AR: 1.50)As a result, Forstag’s liberal bona fides have become a major target. Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez didn’t just stand next to him on a stage last April; they endorsed him in the primary, and Ocasio-Cortez returned to the state to campaign for him, a fact that Republicans are hammering home every chance that they get. In the firefighting offseason, Forstag spent several years lobbying in the Montana State House on behalf of the American Civil Liberties Union, Planned Parenthood and the Montana Library Association.

“Sam Forstag lobbied the Montana Legislature to let men play women’s sports and enter the locker rooms of my girls,” says the voice of the woman in Flint’s most recent campaign ad, referencing Forstag’s lobbying efforts with the ACLU.

In a statement to The Sun, NRCC Spokesman Christian Martinez said “Forstag shamelessly attempted to erase years of his record advocating for radical left groups," and that "Montanans don’t want any part of Forstag’s socialist schemes in the halls of Congress.”

The electorate will likely get very familiar with those lines of attack. One Trump-linked PAC has committed nearly $2 million in advertising spend for October, while a Democrat-linked PAC has committed $1.4 million for the month, according to AdImpact data.

Forstag dismissed the narrative, calling it "disappointing, but not surprising," in a statement. "We have a whole lot of people who are tired of politicians like Aaron trying to pick us apart."

The unanswered question for Democrats in the state is whether Montanans’ obvious frustration with inflation, combined with the loss of longtime federal workers, can stem the state’s rightward shift.

The two polls that show Forstag having a shot are limited in scope: One independent poll taken over Labor Day weekend showed Flint with a one point lead over Forstag, while another Democratic-sponsored poll showed Forstag two percentage points ahead. Both results were well within the margin of error.

On the ground, there are signs that voters are frustrated all around. Visitors at the Dillon Jaycees Pro Rodeo on the Sunday before Labor Day brought up gas prices, inflation and the war in Iran without prompting.

Several attendees told The Washington Sun that they’re so frustrated with costs that they don’t plan to vote at all in November. Or if they do, they don’t know yet who they will vote for.

“Pundits, all of them,” said Beaverhead county resident Josh Bryson, sitting at one of the tables at the fairgrounds behind the rodeo. “I’m feeling pretty disenfranchised.”

And then there are the people who were directly impacted by Trump’s early moves slashing the federal work force. Among them is a woman who was fired in February of 2025 in the middle of chemotherapy treatment for an aggressive cancer. She was a longtime federal worker who had just transferred to a new office in the Forest Service, which technically made her “probationary.”

She was reinstated quickly to her job, but she said the experience changed the way she and her colleagues saw the Forest Service.

“The people who voted for what's happening, I think that they realize now that they shot themselves in the foot,” she said, requesting anonymity as a current government employee.

***

Forstag speaks about smokejumping with an almost cultish reverence. Most jumpers do.

“You’re getting to parachute into the most beautiful corners of the country on the remote stretches of public lands that you can never see otherwise,” he said. “You dig that one trench, cut that line. That fire stops. That’s a rapidly diminishing feeling in modern America, that kind of reward for your labor.”

Smokejumping isn’t a career that firefighters give up lightly. It’s hard to get selected and harder to last. Most recruits wash out during training. When Forstag decided to run for office, he had been with the jumpers for four years. He had health insurance, his income was growing and he loved the work. He wasn’t considering quitting the Forest Service — “absolutely not.”

Trump has changed the way Forstag talks about jumping.

Last summer, Forstag jumped the Crosho fire near Steamboat Springs, Colorado, and landed face-to-face with the aftermath of DOGE.

“I put in an order for pumps and hoses, very basic firefighting stuff. And they tell me, well we used to have a gear cache in Steamboat, but they shut that down. So now we have to overnight airmail the pump and hose setup from Denver,” he said, growing angry as he recounted the story.

He said the team had to pivot to a less efficient plan. “Who benefits from this? It's not the taxpayer. We pay more money. It's not public safety. Public safety is suffering,” he said.

***
The families lining the streets at the Labor Day parade in Dillon, Montana, should not have been Forstag’s kind of crowd. Cattle outnumber humans by more than an 11-to-1 ratio in Beaverhead County. The people who live here went for Trump by more than 40 percentage points in the 2024 election.

But only Smokey the Bear and the spangled Ramblin’ Rose Drill Team got clearly louder cheers than Forstag’s battered 1984 Toyota van, inching its way down North Montana Street on the crisp, windy Monday morning. The campaign ran out of swag halfway down the parade route.

Flint didn’t elicit more obvious enthusiasm from the people along Dillon’s streets.

IMG_3310 copy.jpg (2680x2144, AR: 1.25)Sam Forstag (4032x3024, AR: 1.33)“Everybody is tired of this. They’re getting nothing done,” said longtime Dillon resident Gayle Gransbery, describing politicians in Washington, D.C.

Harris Wheat, another Beaverhead County resident, said he was frustrated with the state of all politics. Then he said he will vote for Forstag in November.

“He’s a working guy. He’s not a politician,” he said. He paused for a long time, and added: “He gets it.”

Walking down the street next to the van plastered in “Sam for Montana” signs was a guy in a faded black smokejumpers T-shirt and a baseball cap that read “God Bless the Rodeo.”

His name is Conor Hogan, another jumper — now an unlikely campaign staffer.

Hogan was never interested in politics before, he said. And he wants nothing to do with it ever again; he’s already applied to go back to jumping next season, regardless of what happens in the election. But for Forstag, a longtime friend and fellow jumper, he quit his summer in the woods.

“Obviously, I'm a kind of biased source, but he's a much better dude than I am,” he said.

IMG_3367 copy.jpg (2873x2299, AR: 1.25)Later that day at the Labor Day picnic in Butte, Montana, Forstag was among allies: In the crowd were unionized government workers, union retirees and union families. Many people got up to sign clipboards when Forstag asked for volunteers to organize for his campaign.

But there were also some faces new to the political scene. Hovering behind the picnic tables was a young man who works for the federal government. He, too, said he doesn’t care for politics, but this time he’s looking forward to voting. Forstag understands how hard the Trump administration has made the job, he said.

Do Forstag’s former smokejumper colleagues feel the same? Enough to vote for him? Hogan laughed.

“It’s an absurd question,” he said.

“If you work your whole life in public lands, right now it's a pretty constant topic of conversation, the fact that they are under attack,” he continued. “I do think there are people who, because of that issue, will vote for Sam who might not otherwise. I really do.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 3
entries.summary: This week’s group features outside hitters from CMIT North and Georgetown Day and a setter from Sherwood.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

From a steady setter in Montgomery County to two potent outside hitters from Prince George’s County and D.C., this week’s Players of the Week showcase the diversity of volleyball talent across the DMV area.

Here’s who shined the brightest in a busy week of play:

Ariel Callwood, Junior, Setter, Sherwood

Callwood has keyed a strong start for Sherwood and is one of several key returners to a Warriors team that advanced to the region finals a season ago. The junior, who was named first team all-county last fall, tallied 70 total assists in Sherwood’s first three matches of the season. She then led her team to a resounding victory at the Magruder Invitational last weekend; the Warriors won all five of their tournament matchups without dropping a set. Callwood’s performance earned her all-tournament honors.

“She knows where to deliver the ball, and that’s absolutely critical,” Sherwood Coach Kaitlyn Jain said. “We have the talent, and so having a setter that can recognize that talent and can deliver and execute on it is just an amazing feeling to have as a coach.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

A’vielle Lewis, Sophomore, Outside Hitter, CMIT North

Lewis has been the catalyst of CMIT North’s blazing start in Prince George’s county play. The sophomore outside hitter notched double-digit kills in each of the Tigers’ matches so far this season, including a 19-kill outing against county power Oxon Hill. Lewis racked up kills at an efficient clip —– against the Clippers last week, she committed just two errors and posted a .739 hitting percentage as the Tigers beat Oxon Hill for the first time in program history. Days later against Laurel, she picked up 14 kills on just 17 swings in a dominant 3-0 sweep.

With Lewis in full command of her team’s offense, the Tigers dropped just one set in their first four matches.

“It’s kind of terrifying when she hits the ball,” CMIT Coach Mark Snyder said. “She’s just a competitor, she wants to win at all costs. … If the game’s on the line, she wants to be the person to get the ball.”

Alexa Telly, Senior, Outside Hitter, Georgetown Day

Telly has picked up right where she left off for the defending DCSAA and ISL champion Hoppers. The senior outside hitter posted 25 kills and 23 digs in a four-set victory over Flint Hill last week. Two days later, the Hoppers picked up a dominant 3-0 sweep over Maret.

With Telly, who is committed to American University, and senior Columbia commit Zora Dimbo providing a dominant one-two punch along the outside, Coach Brandon Wiest’s team looks to once again be a top contender in city and league play.

“[Telly] was insane, unstoppable,” Wiest said of Telly’s performance against Flint Hill. “Everyone in the gym knew she was getting the ball and she was able to score pretty consistently.”

entries.title: DOJ Lists the Stories That Sparked Trump’s Press Ban
entries.summary: Articles on White House ballroom construction, the Iran war and attendance at the Republican midterm convention all made the list.
entries.content:
The Justice Department defended President Donald Trump’s decision to ban several news outlets from the White House grounds, listing a number of stories in a court filing late Tuesday night as examples of the ways that the outlets had jeopardized national security.

The White House Press Office itemized the stories in letters to each individual publication as a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents,” including coverage that allegedly “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods.” Trump last week announced the ban, which affected journalists from three publications: CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," lawyers for the DOJ wrote in the Tuesday filing.

A majority of the stories contained contents revealing munitions and interceptor shortages due to the Iran war, as well as proposed security improvements to the White House ballroom project championed by the president. Other stories included a critical report on low attendance at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, an alleged FBI leak investigation focusing on a journalist and an account of an apparent U.S. military strike on an Iranian school.

The White House ban was the latest escalation in Trump’s war on the press. White House officials previously excluded the Associated Press from events due to its decision to continue using the name “Gulf of Mexico,” demanded Pentagon reporters sign “pledges” to not report information that hasn’t been approved for release and used the Federal Communications Commission to enact what critics have called a pressure campaign against broadcast television stations whose coverage Trump has objected to.

The Justice Department said President Donald Trump’s ban must be upheld because he has “‘compelling interest [s]’ in enforcing minimum standards for bona fide journalists and safeguarding national security information,” the court documents said.

Trump announced the ban Sept. 18 over what he called “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He later told reporters, “Something is wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories.” The White House revoked access to reporters the next day.

CNN, MSNow and Politico argued in a joint complaint Monday that the ban “could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment” and that it was enacted without due process. The administration countered in legal filings Wednesday that the outlets’ due process claims should be dismissed because “they have received adequate notice and post-deprivation process,” referring to the letters sent Tuesday to the outlets that gave them until Friday to contest the decision.

The White House identified four critical stories in its letter to CNN, three in its letter to MSNOW and six to Politico, listed below:

  • A January 2026 CNN story about “top-secret” construction details related to the East Wing bunker.
  • A July 2026 CNN story that the “Trump Administration was ‘struggling to reconcile exactly where things stand’ on munitions counts.”
  • An August 2026 CNN story where “‘multiple sources’ claimed the U.S. military had exhausted nearly 80% of its interceptors.”
  • A September 2026 CNN story that “falsely reported an Iranian school was struck because of ‘outdated intelligence.”
  • A May 2026 MS NOW report “on an alleged leak investigation that the FBI was conducting focusing on a journalist.”
  • A June 2026 MS NOW report where “a source said that President Trump ‘underestimated the willingness of Iran to resume conflict.’”
  • An August 2026 MS NOW story on how “the Iran conflict had ‘significantly depleted’ the US military’s munitions supply.”
  • An April 2025 Politico story “claiming Secretary Rubio and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff were considering lifting sanctions on Russia.”
  • A May 2026 Politico story on a “document detailing funding for the White House ballroom.”
  • An August 2026 Politico report sourced to “a person familiar with Defense Department planning” that said “reduced US military presence in the Pacific and Europe ‘has threatened the Pentagon’s influence around the world.’”
  • An August 2026 Politico report where “a ‘source’” said “the operations in Iran had exhausted US stockpiles of long-range missiles.”
  • A June 2026 Politico story where a “‘senior administration official … granted anonymity’ said the odds of a preliminary deal to end the conflict with Iran were between 80 and 85 percent.” 
  • A September 2026 Politico Playbook report that “relied on unnamed sources to paint the Republican midterm convention in Dallas as a disaster. Media reporting showed that the convention had over 100 million live stream views.”

entries.title: Secret Service to Close Downtown Roads Through Friday for Xi’s State Visit
entries.summary: Drivers should avoid areas near the Waldorf Astoria hotel and expect changing road closures throughout the week.
entries.content:
The Secret Service announced significant road closures in downtown Washington through Friday ahead of President Donald Trump’s state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Waldorf Astoria.

Commuters can expect rolling closures between Joint Base Andrews and the downtown area during the Wednesday commute as part of a series of security measures for Xi’s state visit.

Pennsylvania Ave. between Ninth and 13th Streets NW and 12th Street between Constitution Avenue and E Street NW are closed until 5 p.m. Friday, according to the Metropolitan Police Department. Drivers should also avoid the 12th Street tunnel and downtown portions of 10th and 11th streets, which will also be closed in segments.

Additional closures Thursday will affect Constitution Avenue between 14th and 18th streets NW, along with 15th and 17th streets between Independence Avenue SW and H Street NW, from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m.

On Friday, officials will close the Ninth Street tunnel and stretches of Constitution and Pennsylvania avenues from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Police warned that vehicles violating emergency parking restrictions will be ticketed and towed.

entries.title: Missouri Redistricting Clash Returns to the Supreme Court
entries.summary: The appeal is the third time the court is set to weigh in on Republicans' push to target one Democratic district in Missouri.
entries.content:
The legal drama over Missouri’s congressional districts reached the Supreme Court for a third time on Tuesday night, setting up the justices to deliver the final word on which map the state will use in the midterms.

Opponents of a redrawn map asked the high court to once again block an order from a lower court judge that would require the state to use a map Republicans drew that targeted a Democratic-held seat.

The Supreme Court asked for a response from Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins and the two Republican candidates by 2 p.m. Wednesday.

Election law experts expect the justices will once again rule in a way that requires the state to use a map from 2022 instead, as they did in the two previous times they were asked to weigh in earlier this month.

A federal appeals court on Monday gave new life into the party’s push for the more GOP-friendly map, ruling that the new map should be used unless the Supreme Court steps in within a week.

In a filing to the high court, People Not Politicians, the advocacy group opposed to redistricting, argue that the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling violated the Supreme Court’s prior order.

The group also said that the 8th Circuit lacked the jurisdiction to handle the case in the first place and that Missouri election officials have already begun using the 2022 map. It asked the court to tell the state to use the 2022 maps in the general election.

The lawyers for People Not Politicians wrote that the 8th Circuit ordered the district court to issue a new injunction to use the new maps even though the Supreme Court stayed the first order.

“This Court’s stays are not invitations for a lower court to repackage the same relief and try again,” the lawyers for group wrote.

Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles who focuses on election law, told The Washington Sun that he expects the Supreme Court to decide the same way it did earlier, noting that “this one is incredibly easy.”

Levitt pointed out that when the Supreme Court last paved the way for the state to use the 2022 map on Sept. 10, there were no public dissents. For Levitt, all of the reasons the court ruled as it did that time have only gotten stronger.

“Nothing has changed in Missouri's favor,” Levitt said. “In addition to that, several things got notably worse for the state. Voting has started in the state. Ballots are out. So if the objection was ‘Well the timing was just too tight’ back then, it has gotten well past too tight right now.”

Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown Law professor, wrote that he had no doubt that the challengers to the new map would ask the Supreme Court to step in. “And I have very little doubt that the Supreme Court — yes, even this Supreme Court — will grant it,” he wrote.

Vladeck also pointed out that “if there had been any appetite in the Supreme Court for these kinds of shenanigans” it would have shown up in the Sept. 10 ruling, yet there were no public dissents.

“That suggests that no justice was publicly willing to upend Missouri’s congressional districts at this late hour—or to let a lower federal court override the Missouri Supreme Court’s construction of its own state law,” Vladeck wrote.

Missouri has been entangled in a legal back-and-forth over what the congressional district lines will look like since Republicans ushered a new map through the state legislature last September. Republicans drew out Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s 5th District seat, splitting Kansas City into three congressional districts and giving them a likely 7-1 map.

The state’s GOP was one of the first to redraw their congressional map at the request of President Donald Trump, who pushed for Republicans to make their U.S. House districts more favorable to the party.

Missouri voters used the 2025 redrawn map in the states’ August primary election.

The state began in-person absentee voting on Tuesday. Ballots began going out to out of state eligible voters on Friday.

Those ballots were sent using the 2022 maps, which are in use as the court action is pending.

entries.title: Clyburn Isn’t ‘Confident’ in Democrats' Chances to Win the Majority
entries.summary: The South Carolina Democrat said the party needs “boots on the ground” to reach key voters ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
Rep. Jim Clyburn says Democrats need to fix their voter-targeting methods while looking to mobilize Black voters ahead of the midterms, as the party deals with the aftermath of the Supreme Court decision that paved the way for the elimination of majority-Black congressional districts.

“We've always had a good message, that's not the problem,” Clyburn said on the latest episode of The Washington Sun Cast. “The problem is the messaging. … Our problem has been with our methods, the methods that we use to convey the message.”

Clyburn is taking part in the Congressional Black Caucus Institute’s “So Vote” initiative, which is looking to mobilize turnout among Black voters in the midterms by using community action rather than advertising.

“Why are we dependent upon television to do it when we ought to put boots on the ground,” Clyburn said. “What is it when you pay somebody 20% to place a TV ad from their air-conditioned office? Ain't nobody saying anything about that. And we lose in those elections when you do that.”

“We keep saying to people, ‘Make a plan.’ You're gonna make a plan on TV? How do you make a plan to vote? And so that's what we were trying to do,” Clyburn said.

The April Supreme Court decision in Louisiana v. Callais weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which protected and sometimes mandated majority-minority House districts. Following the decision, several states in the South moved to eliminate districts long held by Black lawmakers.

Clyburn said redistricting was made possible by the loss of state legislative seats by Democrats in years with low Black turnout, and that he is hoping voters reverse those trends.

“This redistricting is going on because we lost legislative seats,” Clyburn said. “What I've been trying to do is respond to history here.”

Clyburn gave a stern “no” when asked if he has confidence Democrats will win the House majority in November, but he said he is encouraged by the work being done on the campaign trail.

“I'm confident that we're going to put forth our best effort, and we will win this majority if everybody really goes to work in an effective way,” Clyburn said.

If Democrats win the House majority, their leadership team is likely to be composed of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California; none of them represent districts in the South.

Clyburn said that makeup will be “different” but not “fatal” when managing the House Democratic Caucus.

“Hakeem Jeffries comes from New York, but his parents, if my memory serves, come from Virginia,” Clyburn said. “I suspect that he has sufficient background. He holds membership in an African American Baptist church there in Brooklyn. I've been to church with him in Brooklyn, New York, so I know and feel strongly that he has what it takes to be a good leader, and he is.”

After serving as the third-ranking Democrat in the House for more than 15 years, Clyburn said he hopes Jeffries will take his thoughts into consideration if he serves as House speaker next session.

“I would hope he would take my background and experiences into account if I express any opinions to him,” Clyburn said. “I may not have any need to express an opinion, but if I see the need to express an opinion, I will. And I would hope he would take it for what it's worth.”

The Washington Sun Cast is a weekly podcast where Washington Sun reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here.

entries.title: Democrats Are Using 'Shadow Hearings' to Go on Offense on ICE
entries.summary: Polls say most voters think immigration enforcement has gone too far, giving Democrats a rare advantage on an issue that hurt them in 2024.
entries.content:
Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Rep. Robert Garcia had already scheduled the latest Democratic public forum on immigration agents’ use of force when an officer shot a Venezuelan immigrant on Sunday.

For nearly three hours in a Senate office building Tuesday, Democrats gave a platform to family members of those fatally shot as part of the Trump administration’s aggressive push on immigration enforcement. They also made the case that no accountability would come unless Democrats regain power.

“I also feel your anger, and we should share that anger, and it is anger that should be directed at the administration,” Blumenthal said to Sean Murphy, an attorney representing the family and estate of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July. “But it also ought to be directed at Congress.”

The forum was one of a dozen unofficial “shadow hearings” Democrats have hosted since late last year, in the Capitol and in states where shootings have taken place. With Americans souring on President Donald Trump’s handling of immigration, Democrats see a rare avenue to resonate with voters on an issue that devastated them in the 2024 election.

On Tuesday, Sen. Alex Padilla of California previewed action to come from the party. “We're all committed to accountability in all its forms, and when we get the gavels back, we're going to move on that aggressively, starting with the investigations,” he said.

And Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas, who lost her bid for the Senate, put it more plainly: “It is time to vote them out,” she said.

Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine hosted one of the field hearings in Biddeford after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed Guerrero, a Colombian national who wasn’t the target of the ICE operation. She said the hearings served as a way to prove to voters that Democrats would seek accountability.

“It is a huge issue in the midterm, absolutely,” Pingree said Tuesday. “And people will have high expectations if Democrats take control of the House, or the House and Senate, that we're going to do something about it.”

Sen. Susan Collins, the Maine Republican in a reelection dogfight, has called on ICE to enact more reforms beyond the recent equipping of agents with body cameras. And a source close to the longtime senator recently told The Washington Sun that of all the potential administration-induced impediments that could crop up, a second ICE shooting is the one that worries them the most and could be too difficult to overcome.

During the unofficial hearings, Democrats have been honing a message on Trump’s immigration crackdown that seeks to incorporate an issue polls show voters are even more concerned about than immigration: corruption. That has become a central topic in competitive House and Senate races.

“This kind of personal account will raise awareness about ICE's corruption and provide an impetus for action after the election,” Blumenthal, of Connecticut, told The Sun after the forum. Blumenthal and Garcia, of California, have held five of the hearings.

Sarah Pierce, who handles immigration issues for the centrist Democratic group Third Way, said Democrats “need to criticize this administration and the radically horrendous things that they're committing in the name of immigration enforcement.”

“But they need to do so in a way that doesn't allow voters to associate them with a lack of any sort of immigration enforcement,” Pierce said. “There's this Biden hangover that Democrats are fighting against.”

The mothers of Renee Good and Ruben Martinez, both shot and killed by ICE agents, said during the Tuesday forum that they voted for Trump.

“I did vote for him, and that is something that I truly regret,” said Martinez’s mom, Rachel Reyes. “A lot of Americans feel like me right now, especially the Latin community. It's just awful. We haven't heard anything from any Republican whatsoever.”

That sentiment is reflected in recent polling. A Fox News poll this month found that 60% of Hispanic voters think immigration enforcement has gone too far, with 53% of all voters saying the same. The majority of all voters, 55%, and of independent voters, 58%, disapprove of the president’s handling of immigration, according to an Ipsos poll conducted last week.

Democratic strategist Maria Cardona said linking corruption to the violent tactics of immigration agents and the lowering of ICE’s training standards, the subject of one of the February forums, appeals to a broader range of voters.

“Yes, it's about the cruelty of how they carry out these enforcement mechanisms, but the issue of corruption, the issue of this being a huge abuse of power, a huge waste of taxpayer money — all of those issues are critical in helping the American voter understand that this is not what they voted for,” she said.

Political strategist Chuck Rocha views the Democrats’ approach to ICE ahead of the midterms as a message on corruption rather than immigration. While he said there’s “no doubt” that it will be effective in the midterms, Democrats would soon have to come up with a plan if they win control.

“You don't see anybody rolling out what the solution they have for whatever immigration policy A, B or C is,” Rocha said. “We need to get some details done and show people what we're for, not just what we're against.”

entries.title: White House Denies a Report that Trump Wants to Put His Name on Ford’s Theatre
entries.summary: The historic venue is owned by the Interior Department.
entries.content:
The White House denied a report on Wednesday that President Donald Trump is considering adding his name to Ford’s Theatre as part of his push to put his mark on the city.

MS NOW reported earlier Wednesday that the administration has a list of sites that could bear the president’s name, including Ford’s Theatre, citing anonymous sources within the administration.

The theater — best known as the site of former President Abraham Lincoln’s assasination — is owned by the Interior Department and maintained by the National Park Service.

The Interior Department told The Washington Sun in a statement that the report “is not true.”

The White House also denied that any such plan is in the works.

“This story is completely false. The reality is that failing MS Now continues to push false and baseless claims from anonymous sources who have no clue what they’re talking about, which is exactly why their credibility is in the toilet. It is embarrassing to watch,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to The Sun.

The administration has targeted MS NOW, along with Politico and CNN, with a ban from the White House for reporting what Trump called “fake news.”

The Ford’s Theatre Society did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ford’s Theatre first opened as a Baptist church in 1834 before transitioning to a performance venue in the 1860s. It’s now a working venue and museum.

Trump has made multiple attempts to physically cement his presidential legacy in the capital region. Along with the U.S. Institute of Peace headquarters and the Kennedy Center, Trump has alluded to slapping his name on Dulles International Airport in Virginia and the new Commanders’ Stadium in Southeast D.C.

entries.title: Wes Moore Rolls Out New Regulations for Maryland Data Center Projects
entries.summary: Moore said Wednesday that he would "immediately" begin working with the state’s General Assembly to repeal a tax exemption for data centers passed in 2020.
entries.content:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore on Wednesday signed an executive order imposing stricter regulation on data center development in the state.

In doing so, the state joined a broader bipartisan effort that is taking place across the country, in which states — citing the federal government’s inaction — are trying to regulate data centers through executive action.

“Since Donald Trump returned to office, his administration has moved fast to roll back critical safeguards, giving Big Tech more room to determine their own destiny,” said Moore, who is considered a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender. “Truthfully, the people are fed up, and so am I.”

The order would require community and state approval for data center development as well as encourage private investment and financing to ensure that taxpayers do not end up bankrolling the facilities’ energy costs. Moore’s order also requires developers to comply with environmental guidelines.

Moore added Wednesday that he would "immediately" begin working with the state’s General Assembly to repeal a tax exemption passed in 2020 that provides data center developers with tax-funded incentives to build their operations in Maryland.

“Our families come first, and our children come first. Not a developer's timeline, and not a corporation's bottom line. And we will use every tool that we have at our disposal to make sure that no family and no community is left behind,” Moore said.

A Pew Research Poll found that Americans’ views on data centers have soured, with 60% of Americans saying “they would be not too or at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area.”

Maryland is the latest state to join the effort. Over the last few weeks, Texas, Virginia and Pennsylvania's state governments have also announced temporary development pauses, stricter permitting rules and new utility requirements as the facilities’ demands on electricity, water and local infrastructure become a political issue.

On Monday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed state environmental regulators to halt permits for data center projects while state officials conduct audits of their impacts on the electric grid and water resources.

Last week, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order banning nondisclosure agreements involving data center projects, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order requiring data center developers seeking state permits to make legally binding commitments on energy costs while removing the projects from the state’s fast-track permitting program.

While more states move to rein in data center developers, President Donald Trump, who has spent the last couple of weeks feuding with artificial intelligence leaders, has shown little interest in rolling out regulations to address the public’s concerns.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted to Truth Social late last month.

entries.title: The Top Group Fighting Trump’s Ballroom Announces a New Legal Defense Fund
entries.summary: The National Trust for Historic Preservation said the fund would provide it with resources to counter “current and emerging threats.”
entries.content:
The leading preservationist group fighting President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom construction project announced a multimillion-dollar fundraising campaign Wednesday to use for legal defense.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation’s $10 million fund, dubbed the “Historic Preservation Defense Fund,” will boost the group’s “legal defense, public advocacy, and community action whenever historic places and the laws that protect them are under threat,” the group said in a statement.

“This is an urgent, pivotal moment for historic preservation. Our nation’s iconic, historic buildings and places, and with them the foundational stories of our country, are now under a generational threat,” National Trust President and CEO Brent Leggs said Wednesday at an event.

He said the funds will be used to provide “investment and support for a united preservation movement” to counter what the organization called “current and emerging threats.”

The National Trust sued the Trump administration in December 2025 to halt the construction of the White House ballroom, which the president has argued is needed to safely host large-scale events. The ballroom is one of many projects Trump has undertaken to beautify D.C. through his gilded aesthetics.

The National Trust argued in court filings that the ballroom was an unlawful project that skipped over a federal review process and congressional approval.

The Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court after lower courts ruled to stop construction. The Supreme Court issued an unsigned opinion in August that allowed the project to continue, saying the federal government is likely to prevail in showing the National Trust did not have the legal right to challenge the ballroom’s construction. The opinion also added that if construction were stopped, national security would be harmed.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote a dissent, joined by the three liberal justices, that said the construction “is likely unlawful.” Trump celebrated the victory on Truth Social at the time and said the facility will be unveiled in the summer of 2028.

entries.title: Oklahoma Republicans Are at War Over Who Finishes Mullin’s Senate Term
entries.summary: The acting senator and the likely 2026 election winner both think the job is theirs until January.
entries.content:
An internal fight between Oklahoma's appointed senator and likely successor is boiling over as both Republicans vie to fill the last two months of former Sen. Markwayne Mullin's term.

The dispute is over when Sen. Alan Armstrong’s temporary term ends and the next Oklahoma senator — likely Rep. Kevin Hern — would be sworn in.

Hern wants to be sworn into the Senate in November following the election, while Armstrong wants to stay on through January.

According to Oklahoma law, “The candidate elected to the office at the regularly scheduled election shall be deemed to also have been elected to fill the vacancy and shall be eligible to assume the office upon the official certification of the election by the State Election Board.”

Another section of the law reads, “When a vacancy occurs in the office of a member of the United States Senate from Oklahoma, the Governor shall, within thirty (30) days of occurrence of the vacancy: Appoint a person eligible to hold such office, who has been a registered voter of the party of the predecessor in Oklahoma for at least five (5) years preceding the date that the vacancy was created, to serve in such office until a successor is elected.”

According to multiple sources familiar with the matter, Hern’s team believes the law would allow Hern — if he wins the election — to be sworn into the Senate in November, as Oklahoma must certify the election within seven days of it being completed. However, Armstrong’s team believes the law is less clear and that he was appointed to serve out the remainder of now Secretary of Homeland Security Mullin’s term, which ends in early January.

Armstrong wants to stay on at least until legislation on permitting reform gets done, sources tell The Washington Sun. There’s a chance that happens in the lame-duck session.

All this has caused a rift between the two members, sources say.

Hern has hired prominent Oklahoma attorney Glenn Coffee to help with any challenge to him taking office in November, sources tell The Sun, while Armstrong has Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt on his side pushing for him to remain in office until January.

On Sept.11, an attorney representing Armstrong sent a letter, which The Sun obtained, to Stitt asking that he request the attorney general’s opinion on the matter.

In the letter, the lawyer says, “The upcoming Senate election is not intended to determine who will succeed to the few remaining weeks” of the term.

Armstrong’s attorney said that “Senator Armstrong seeks an opinion addressing whether his appointment continues until the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, or terminates immediately upon certification and qualification of a new Senator elected at the upcoming election.”

Multiple sources told The Sun that Stitt has not yet requested the attorney general’s opinion on the matter.

However on Tuesday, State Senate Pro Tempore Lonnie Paxton requested an opinion from state Attorney General Gentner Drummond on when the next senator would get sworn in.

“I write to request the Attorney General's formal opinion on three questions concerning the proper application of that statutory scheme to a vacancy currently pending in Oklahoma's United States Senate delegation,” reads a copy of the request obtained by The Sun. “Questions have been raised regarding whether 51 O.S. § 15, a general statute addressed to appointed officers generally, may extend an appointee's tenure beyond the point a successor is elected under § 10(C), and regarding the scope of the Governor's duties once that election has occurred and been certified. Because this question bears directly on the orderly administration of a pending statutory succession, and because I am aware of no prior formal opinion addressing it, I believe the Attorney General's guidance would serve the public interest and would assist the Legislature in evaluating whether any further clarifying legislation is warranted.”

The request has three questions they want the Attorney General to answer:

“Does 51 O.S. § 15's provision that ‘every appointed officer shall hold his office until the end of the term for which the officer whom he succeeds was elected or appointed, and until his successor is elected and qualified’ extend the tenure of a Governor-appointed United States Senator beyond the point a successor is elected, where 51 O.S. § 10(C) separately provides that such an appointee serves only ‘until a successor is elected’”

“Does 26 O.S. § 12-101(C)(3)'s provision that a candidate ‘shall be deemed to also have been elected to fill the vacancy and shall be eligible to assume the office upon the official certification of the election by the State Election Board’ require any additional act, beyond that certification, before the winning candidate is entitled to assume the office?”

“Does the Governor retain any discretion under Oklahoma or federal law to decline or delay performing that certification once the State Election Board has certified the results of the election?”

How Drummond would opine on this case is unknown. But both sides are hopeful that he will rule in their favor and believe the law is on their side.

In a statement, Miranda Dabney, a spokesperson for Armstrong, said that “Senator Armstrong was proud to be appointed by Governor Stitt to fill the vacancy for the remainder of the 119th Congress. We have reviewed state law and sought legal guidance. There is no vacancy to be filled. We remain committed to advancing permitting reform. Should Rep. Hern prevail in the election, we look forward to him being seated in the 120th Congress, along with his colleagues.”

A spokesperson for Hern said that “Congressman Hern is focused on winning in November.”

“From day one, he has followed the process articulated by Oklahoma law which clearly provides that a temporary appointment in the U.S Senate only lasts until the vacancy is ‘filled by election as provided by law.’ Any intentional delay in that process would subvert the will of the voters and Oklahoma law. We believe that any independent legal opinion or judicial review would confirm that the law is clear,” the spokesperson for Hern said in the statement.

The quote the spokesperson references is a portion of Stitt’s official appointment of Armstrong where he appoints “Alan Armstrong, a Senator from said State to represent said State in the Senate of the United States until the vacancy therein caused by the resignation of Markwayne Mullin, is filled by election as provided by law.”

entries.title: Trump's Board of Peace Proposes a $2.45B Blueprint to Kick-Start Gaza Reconstruction
entries.summary: The plan includes 66 projects that it hopes to accomplish, including infrastructure, education and health initiatives.
entries.content:
By Matthew Lee

NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S.-backed Board of Peace is proposing a six-month, $2.45 billion plan to begin reconstruction and governance in Gaza as President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan struggles to stay afloat.

At a meeting of the group’s board in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, the governors unveiled a 66-project blueprint to get things started while acknowledging enormous hurdles that must still be overcome. The projects include ambitious infrastructure, education and health initiatives that are designed to support Trump’s 20-point plan to end the Israel-Hamas war.

“The need is immense,” the board said, noting that full reconstruction from the physical damage across Gaza will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next 10 years.

The proposal is largely aimed at potential donors who will be asked to foot the bill for reconstruction of the war-devastated territory.

The ceasefire, which took effect on Oct. 10, was meant to clear the way for a broader process to rebuild Gaza under the guidance of the Board of Peace. The plan included additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas, the arrival of an international peacekeeping force and a new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory’s day-to-day affairs. It also envisioned an ambitious program for rebuilding war-ravaged Gaza.

But the U.S.-backed plan has largely stalled. While the ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting and humanitarian conditions have improved, the Israeli military has expanded its control of Gaza and now occupies some 60% of the territory. Hamas has not given up its weapons. The international military force and new government still have not entered Gaza, and reconstruction has not begun. The vast majority of Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes.

The board’s high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said progress hinges largely on Hamas disarming — a step the group has refused to take. But he also has pressed Israel to scale back its military operation.

“I want to be very clear that we are not bound by a calendar,” he said. “We want to make sure that this works.”

Key questions that the board faces are not only laying out plans for reconstruction but also a timeline for the deployment of the international force meant to provide security in the territory and a new government, plans to disarm Hamas, and bringing in badly needed building materials.

U.S. Gen. Jasper Jeffers, commander of the international stabilization force planned for Gaza, outlined a five-step approach to dealing with the thorny issue of demilitarizing Hamas. It begins with the first wave of the multinational unit being deployed with troops from Kosovo and Morocco, to be followed by additional personnel from Albania and Kazakhstan.

Their task will be to demilitarize the territory and decommission all of Hamas’ military infrastructure.

The goal, he said, is to gradually turn security control over to the interim government, after which Israel will be expected to withdraw its forces.

___

Associated Press writers Josef Federman and Julia Frankel in Jerusalem and Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

entries.title: U.S. Diplomat Walks Out of Iranian President’s Defiant U.N. Speech
entries.summary: They appeared to be the only U.S. representative present for Masoud Pezeshkian’s address.
entries.content:
A representative for the U.S. stormed out of a defiant speech by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Wednesday at the United Nations General Assembly, during which he defended his country’s efforts in the ongoing war against the U.S. and lambasted President Donald Trump for “bullying” the Iranian people.

The official left just as Pezeshkian held up photos of people killed in the war — including Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and students from the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, who were killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes when the war broke out Feb. 28.

“Yesterday the United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism. I come from an Iran in which our esteemed supreme leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason. I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school. You see these children? These children perished under bombs with weapons used by the United States and Israel,” Pezeshkian said, according to a translation of his address.

The U.S. representative who walked out appeared to be the only U.S. diplomat present for Pezeshkian’s address. They weren't the only one who staged a walkout this week: the Cuban delegation abruptly walked out of Trump’s speech on Tuesday after he mentioned ongoing negotiations with its government.

Pezeshkian ultimately said his country will not cave to a “language of force” but is ready for “dialog and diplomacy and negotiations.”

Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran just a day prior during his own address to the U.N., and called on the international body to unite and eradicate what he called the “51-year menace of Iranian terror.”

Pezeshkian hit back Wednesday against Trump’s characterization of his country. 

“We are sanctioned. We are punished. Those who are ill, innocent people, the poor, the least privileged in our society are the targets of these sanctions. And this is what the United States seeks to do with all countries: to sacrifice the population of a country in order to achieve her illegitimate goals,” he said.

The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but broader negotiations to end the war appeared to stall as the two countries returned to fighting when the ceasefire collapsed. 

U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner engaged with Iranian officials in an hourslong talk on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York this week. Trump described the meeting as “very good” and said another talk is set to be “scheduled in the very near future.”

The Trump administration has repeatedly said that one of the U.S.’s main goals is to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon. Pezeshkian declared on Wednesday that Iran “will not bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours,” when speaking about the country’s domestic nuclear program. 

He also argued that Iran had built up its weapons capabilities in order to defend themselves from adversaries, while maintaining that his country does “not seek anyone's permission or approval” in order to defend their nation. 

The Iranian president also spent a good portion of the address criticizing Israel for “savagely murdering” tens of thousands of people in Gaza, as well as the country’s role in the ongoing war.

“Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions. This is a true tragedy, which would make anyone hearing it laugh, at best,” Pezeshkian said.

Iran is currently under heavy U.S. sanctions impacting its economic and energy sectors — with the penalties citing the country's support for terrorism, concerns over nuclear proliferation and human rights abuses. 

Pezeshkian argued that the international community deploys “double standard” for monitoring Iran and Israel’s nuclear capabilities. 

“Israel has the bombs, has weapons of mass destruction, is not a member of the Non-Proliferation Treaty, during her shameful life has not allowed a single inspection, but they are rewarded by all the means necessary for them to be able to bomb any capital in the region at will,” Pezeshkian said. 

Iran and 191 other countries are party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, an agreement signed decades ago to prevent the global spread of nuclear weapons. The International Atomic Energy Agency, which operates independently but reports to the U.N., is charged with inspecting and accounting for nuclear material. 

Israel is not part of the NPT, so the country is not subject to the same IAEA inspection as Iran — though Israel is believed to be one of the nine countries that has access to nuclear weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

entries.title: Trump’s Touting a Ballroom Drone Port — But There’s Already One Next Door
entries.summary: A few hundred feet away, a drone port, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, is already quietly operational.
entries.content:
By Collin Binkley

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops, ostensibly to protect the 18-acre complex and the nation’s capital.

A few hundred feet away, a drone port, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, is already quietly operational. Equipped with cameras and sensors to scope out potential threats from a bird’s-eye view, the small UAVs stand on alert in four gray weatherproof boxes until deployed at officers' commands.

The agency is using a model known as “drone as first responder,” deploying speedy unarmed drones from outdoor stations to serve as flying cameras. That model has been adopted by hundreds of police agencies across the U.S., often powered by AI software to help dodge obstacles or track targets.

The existence of the surveillance drones on a Treasury Department building adjacent to the White House complex has not been previously reported, and could undercut Trump's legal claims that the ballroom construction is necessary “to protect the White House and surrounding region from aerial attacks.” The need for the drone port underpinned Trump's national security defense for the construction project — a justification he is now citing for the construction of a massive arch outside the gates of Arlington National Cemetery.

The installation is thus far markedly less imposing than the vision outlined by Trump, with its rows of futuristic attack drones, apparently modeled after those used in U.S. military strikes, that drone experts describe as outlandish.

“To be honest, if a drone was so close to the White House that it needed interdiction, it’s already gotten too far,” said Matt Sloane, co-founder of SkyfireAI, which makes software for drones used by public safety agencies.

It would be more realistic for the White House to build something akin to what the Secret Service is using next door, Sloane said: “The drone takes off and does some type of perimeter sweep or whatever, and then puts itself back in the box.”

The White House did not comment for the story. The Secret Service declined to comment on the specifics of its drone operations but said the new docks are separate from Trump's ballroom drone port.

The details of Trump’s ballroom drone port remain murky

Security of the president and the White House complex is generally the domain of the Secret Service, which works in close concert with the White House Military Office and other military elements when needed.

Trump has said the drone port came at the request of U.S. military officials. Speaking to reporters in May, he said the building’s plans were expanded to meet the request: “They wanted more drone capacity,” he said. On social media, he boasted that the drone port might end up being the “most sophisticated” in the world.

What Trump is ultimately aiming to build, and how far it goes beyond what has already been installed, remains unclear. Beyond Trump’s AI images, some of which he filed in his appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court to lift lower courts' blocks on the construction, the White House has not disclosed what kinds of drones will be used or for what tactical purpose.

The Secret Service is using smaller surveillance drones that are a fraction of the size of the attack drones depicted in Trump’s AI images. The U.S. Air Force bought similar drones from Skydio in April to protect bases across the Middle East. The company also supplied drones to help protect World Cup matches this year.

The Secret Service has been building out its drone- and counter-drone programs for years. But work has accelerated since the 2024 attempted assassination of Trump at a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, when the agency failed both to take action against a drone used by the shooter to scout out the attack and to fly one of its own to provide overwatch of the event.

In the weeks that followed, tethered and untethered surveillance drones became commonplace at campaign rallies and large events at the White House complex.

In an online video released by the agency highlighting their deployment, the Secret Service said the Skydio drones are used to provide “real-time situational awareness” and “aerial overwatch."

“It allows you to see the threat before it becomes an issue, and to task assets accordingly,” Dustin Talbott, of the Secret Service’s Aviation and Airspace Security Division, said in the video. “We no longer wait for the threat to reveal itself. We find it first.”

Skydio did not provide comment for this story.

Trump's drone port vision would face logistical hurdles

Trump has made it a priority to build a stronger drone presence around the White House, responding to an increase in political violence and the evolution of drone warfare.

Paul Eckloff, a former supervisor of the Secret Service’s presidential protection division, said the Russia-Ukraine war has highlighted the risks posed by drones, even off-the-shelf models that can cause massive damage. Drones now represent one of the largest emerging threats the White House must defend against, he said.

During Trump’s first term, conversations about drones often centered on their use in places like Iraq and Syria, said Javed Ali, who served on the National Security Council during that time and now teaches national security at the University of Michigan. Since then, it has become a matter of domestic security, he said.

Yet there would be major logistical hurdles involved in putting a busy drone port on top of the White House, he said. “There’s a whole host of questions, like who is responsible for overseeing it, and how would there be any de-confliction with commercial airspace?” he said.

Complexities around federal oversight were laid bare this year when the U.S. military used a laser to shoot down a drone near El Paso, Texas, only to find it belonged to Customs and Border Protection. The mishap briefly led the FAA to close nearby airspace.

A drone hub at the White House would navigate crowded and complex airspace around Washington, not far from Reagan Washington National Airport and flight paths shared by other military aircraft.

Opponents say the White House is becoming a fortress

Trump started talking about the drone port in May, weeks after a federal judge halted ballroom construction but allowed work on security components to continue. Trump later went on to refer to the ballroom as a “military complex,” leaning on that security role as a legal justification.

The Supreme Court in August cleared Trump to continue construction as the legal challenge moves ahead.

Opponents say the president is going too far in his hardening of the White House, turning it into something closer to a fortress. Edward Lengel, a former chief historian for the White House Historical Association, said Trump has militarized the White House at a scale that’s at odds with its legacy as “the people’s house.”

“It turns it into a big giant porcupine that has its spines pointing out against the people and against the world,” Lengel said.

Trump has argued that the White House was in “very bad condition” when he returned to office, saying it had become vulnerable to modern threats.

At times, he has expressed concerns about his own safety and the risks posed by drones and other air threats. Speaking at a Rose Garden dinner for law enforcement officials in May, Trump quickly glanced up from the lectern as a low bird flew overhead.

“I thought that was a drone,” Trump said, bringing laughs from the crowd. “They make them in all different sizes nowadays — they can be very destructive, as you’ve probably heard."

entries.title: Sanders Unveils a Bill to Ban Artificial Superintelligence and Create a ‘Department of AI’
entries.summary: Multiple employees at leading AI companies have already endorsed the bill.
entries.content:
By Joey Cappelletti

Two leading progressive lawmakers, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar, are unveiling legislation Wednesday that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI as some of the industry’s own leaders urge Congress to impose guardrails on the advancing technology.

The bill, provided first to The Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill.

"It doesn’t take a genius to say, ‘slow it down,’” Sanders, I-Vt., said in an interview with AP. “Do we really want to develop a super intelligence that when it becomes smarter than human beings could act independently of human control? I don’t think we do.”

Congress has so far done little to rein in the AI industry even as some of its most prominent leaders warn about potentially catastrophic risks. President Donald Trump has resisted recent calls for greater government oversight, putting him at odds with tech leaders including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and xAI’s Elon Musk.

The bill aims to dramatically slow down AI development

The legislation would permanently prohibit artificial superintelligence, which it defines as a system that exceeds human cognitive ability or has sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity.

It would temporarily pause development of the most advanced AI systems until new federal safety rules are established by a new Department of Artificial Intelligence. Advanced AI systems would then need federal approval before they could be deployed. Violations could carry significant penalties, including up to 20 years in prison in some cases.

A number of current employees at AI companies and experts signed on in support of the bill, according to a statement shared with AP.

Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a researcher in OpenAI’s Safety Systems, said in a statement supporting the bill that “superintelligence could either go extremely right or extremely wrong” and that “we shouldn’t be playing such games.”

Swante Scholz, a software engineer at Google DeepMind who said he was not speaking on behalf of his employer, said on the current path of development, the “most likely outcome is an existential catastrophe for humanity.”

“A ban on superintelligence development would be a positive change for the foreseeable future,” Scholz said in a statement.

The bill faces long odds but draws a line in a growing fight

The bill from Sanders and Casar faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress, where lawmakers have struggled to coalesce around even less sweeping AI regulations.

But it offers a window into how the progressive wing of the Democratic Party is approaching AI regulation ahead of November’s midterms and a 2028 presidential campaign in which the technology is expected to be an increasingly prominent issue. Casar, a Democrat from Texas, is the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

Potential 2028 presidential candidates have rushed in recent weeks to release proposals showing they're taking the issue seriously. Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore announced a plan to regulate AI on Tuesday, while California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order to accelerate implementation of a California law that calls for independent oversight of AI companies last week.

Sanders, a two-time presidential candidate who is now 85, has especially focused on the issue in recent months. In June, he introduced legislation to create a sovereign wealth fund financed through a one-time tax on the stock of the largest AI companies. Last week, he hosted colleagues for a briefing with experts and also attended a conference focused on the issue alongside Republicans, including former White House adviser Steve Bannon.

The debate over AI regulations has scrambled political alliances both in Washington and for voters across the country.

Americans have grown more concerned about the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence over the last year, according to a recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago.

The survey data say about half, 53%, of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about artificial intelligence’s environmental impacts. That is up from 41% last year. Democrats are driving much of the increase in environmental concern, but the poll also reveals broader worries about the local impact of data centers, which power AI and cloud computing.

Trump has shown little interest in curbing AI risks

While some industry leaders have called for new safeguards, Trump has pushed in the opposite direction. On Tuesday, Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that artificial intelligence will be renamed “super intelligence."

“I think Trump has very little understanding of what this issue is about,” Sanders said. “I think he’s mainly concerned about the economic implications of a slowdown.”

AI safety is expected to be a central part of talks between Trump and China’s Xi Jinping at the White House this week as the countries compete for dominance in the sector. The prospect of slowing development in the United States while China continues on has also been one of the central arguments against sweeping restrictions.

Sanders argued that avoiding the most dangerous forms of AI would ultimately require cooperation between the two countries, comparing the challenge to nuclear arms control during the Cold War.

“Ronald Reagan, arch-conservative, was smart enough to understand that he had to sit down with Gorbachev, a communist, and work out a nuclear treaty that protected humanity,” Sanders said. “I think we can do that again now.”

entries.title: Democrats Block Rand Paul’s Effort to Grant an Ex-Fauci Adviser Immunity
entries.summary: The senator sought to give immunity to Dr. Anthony Fauci’s former assistant to get her to comply with an investigation.
entries.content:
Republican Sen. Rand Paul’s effort to compel Dr. Anthony Fauci's former special assistant to testify in an investigation by granting her an immunity order failed to pass the Senate Homeland Security Committee after every Democrat voted against it.

Paul needed at least two Democrats to support the motion in order to meet the required two-thirds threshold. The failed motion set back Paul’s latest investigation into Fauci, which stems from the senator’s claims that the infectious disease expert lied to the public about the COVID-19 virus’ origins.

The Republican-led probe will continue despite Fauci invoking his right to not self incriminate more than 100 times during a contentious hearing in July, Paul said during the committee hearing. Fauci’s unidentified assistant also invoked her Fifth Amendment rights when she was subpoenaed last week, Paul added.

“She may have that right, but her silence does not end this investigation,” Paul said. “This resolution allows us to ask a federal court to grant her immunity. … We are here today to remove the obstacles she raised so she can answer the committee questions without any fear of conviction.”

Paul said he is specifically seeking more details about what the assistant knew in regards to an email Fauci sent to former World Health Organization Chief Scientist Jeremy Farrar on Jan. 30, 2020, about the virus’ “spike protein.”

On Wednesday, one Democrat voted in person and six others voted by proxy, while all eight of the committee’s Republicans were present to vote in favor of the motion.

“A majority of the committee voted to seek the truth. All Republicans voted to seek the truth,” Paul said after the 8-7 vote divided along party lines. “We voted to protect this witness and hear her story.”

“This is disappointing. It doesn't end here,” Paul said, later pledging to ask the Justice Department to “pursue this,” though he did not give additional details.

In August, Paul asked the Justice Department for the fourth time to investigate Fauci, who was granted preemptive pardon by former President Joe Biden that protects him from federal prosecution.

entries.title: Heads of AI Firms Tell the UN That AI Could Be a Risk to All of Humanity
entries.summary: "I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said.
entries.content:
By Seth Borenstein

UNITED NATIONS — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world — or, at least, its people.

“If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” said Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic.

“We could lose control of the future to AI,” said his competitor, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.

Both said the countries of the world, though the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday afternoon, have to set safeguards, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn’t concentrated in one company or country.

For world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine?

The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday huddled with top technology leaders to figure out if the increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Other lingering questions: How could it be done? When might it be just too late?

The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of “killer robots." Experts and European leaders said that’s not hyperbole but something that’s already a reality or at least perilously close.
