entries.title: Susan Collins’ Campaign Is Eager to Put Corruption Allegations to Rest
entries.summary: The senator is fighting a tough reelection race in a year when corruption is a sticky message.
entries.content:
Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign is fighting to steer clear of corruption accusations after a new report about her campaign contributions.

Collins’ campaign manager, Steve Abbott, answered questions from reporters for 30 minutes on Wednesday about ProPublica’s report that the Maine Republican had been scrutinized by the FBI’s anti-corruption group for awarding government contracts to the defense contractor Navatek after its CEO, Martin Kao, donated to a Collins super PAC.

Collins’ office denied the allegations and told ProPublica that her office “fully cooperated” with the FBI investigation. An FBI spokesperson told ProPublica that the agency “ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign” after investigating the claims years ago.

Both parties have focused their campaign messaging around corruption this year, with the word appearing in dozens of campaign ads. Connecting corruption among politicians to the electorate’s stress with the economy is a persuasive message to voters, strategists told The Washington Sun.

Collins’ campaign attempted to pivot attention to the federal dollars Collins has sent to Maine as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

“I will stay here all day — and don't feel obligated to — but anybody who has any questions about these things, I'm happy to talk to you about them because it's false,” Abbott told reporters in Portland, Maine. “They're allegations from a guy who's awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense who's trying to get his sentence reduced.”

Collins called the story a “partisan hit job” on a Wall Street Journal Opinion podcast on Wednesday hosted by editorial board member Kim Strassel.

“Shame on ProPublica for taking the words of a twice-convicted felon over my office, campaign staff and me,” she said. “It’s disgraceful.”

Collins has been dodging accusations of corruption the entire campaign. Her former opponent, Democrat Graham Platner, alleged that Collins used her position in Congress to send funds to a lobbying firm her husband worked for, which the Collins campaign denied. Platner dropped out of the race the next month over sexual assault allegations. She now faces Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine State Senate.

Abbott also called the allegations “recycled” from the senator’s previous bid.

“We hear this every cycle that Susan Collins is corrupt,” Abbott said. “I mean, whatever. I'm just so, I guess, used to it, and it's so tiresome. It's the same thing over and over and over again.”

entries.title: Two Democratic Senators Will Try to Force a Vote on AI Safety
entries.summary: The push comes amid growing urgency to respond to the rapid growth of AI.
entries.content:
Two Democratic senators are attempting to force a vote Thursday on a bill requiring artificial intelligence firms to submit their new models for government approval.

Sens. Mark Warner of Virginia and Brian Schatz of Hawaii will introduce a bill mandating that frontier companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have the National Security Agency assess their models prior to release. Currently, the Trump administration has set up only an optional regime for testing the models.

Warner and Schatz will attempt to get the bill passed through unanimous consent, a procedure that allows for expedited votes on legislation if every senator agrees.

The push reflects the growing urgency of concerns about the pace of AI development. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) on Wednesday also explored using this mechanism to pass a bill to protect whistleblowers who disclose information about AI risks.

The efforts set the stage for a potential confrontation within the Senate over the risks of AI as the upper chamber prepares to adjourn for recess. The concerns about AI have been magnified in recent weeks by the disclosure of repeated hacking incidents and the high-profile resignation of a researcher at Anthropic.

Warner has been in close contact with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and business leaders such as JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon about the potential risks of AI and the need for federal intervention, a spokesperson said.

The Virginia senator has kept his distance from calls by his liberal colleagues such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) to halt the development of artificial intelligence, calling himself “long-term bullish on AI.” But he and Schatz have pushed for more oversight than the Trump administration is supporting.

Their legislation includes other AI safety measures, such as establishing a federal database for AI safety incidents; directing the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop an AI risk-assessment system; and authorizing the Commerce Department to work with foreign countries on testing, security and reporting.

“I’m less worried about some science-fiction scenario where AI ends humanity than I am about a very real scenario where a powerful AI system breaks into a bank, disrupts a water system, or compromises some other piece of critical infrastructure,” Warner said in a statement. “Those risks aren’t theoretical anymore, and we need to make sure our security and safeguards keep pace with the technology.

entries.title: Loudoun County School Board Adopts a Religiously Diverse Calendar
entries.summary: The decision involved a contentious debate over whether to follow the federal holiday calendar or include religious holidays like Diwali and Rosh Hashanah.
entries.content:
The Loudoun County School Board adopted a religiously diverse calendar for the 2028-29 school year, as opposed to one based on the federal holiday calendar that only included major Christian holidays, by a 5-4 vote and after a contentious debate.

Catoctin District board member Kari Labell, who voted in favor of the federally aligned calendar, argued that, besides Christmas, the diverse calendar was not equitable toward all religions, particularly Christianity.

“Things like Ash Wednesday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday — all of those days are Christian holidays,” Labell said. “There are many, many saints' days that we celebrate in the Christian religion. None of that is accounted for on this calendar. We are not a religious institution. We are an educational institution.”

The 2028-29 calendar includes the Lunar New Year, Diwali, Rosh Hashanah and Eid al-Fitr. Several board members remarked that recognizing these holidays would represent good-faith efforts to respect the diversity of the district.

Board member Ross Svenson represents Broad Run, an area with a heavy Indian American population. He said nearly a “quarter of a class could be absent” during Diwali if the religiously diverse calendar were not accepted, causing disruption for all students and making it harder for teachers to plan.

Svenson added that while there is “no solution that makes everyone happy,” accepting the inclusive calendar was the “right thing to do.”

The board typically approves calendars two years in advance. School districts around the country usually observe federally recognized holidays, but creating calendars is left up to local and state officials.

In Loudoun County, input from community sessions and student, parent and teacher surveys was also considered. Board Chair and Algonkian District member April Chandler said the board received up to 200 emails an hour related to the calendar decision.

Recalling a conversation she’d had with a constituent last school year, Chandler said tests, school assemblies and even field trips scheduled on the major observances of other cultures could force some parents into hard decisions.

“On the second-most important religious holiday in Islam, at one of the schools in my district, there was a field trip scheduled on that day, and in having the conversation with that parent, I was devastated to think about what that decision must be like, to have to step away from your religious observation to choose between school and your religious holiday,” she said.

Sterling District board member Amy Riccardi, who voted in favor of the federally aligned calendar, argued that students are allowed excused absences for religious reasons. She said constituents affected by a precarious regional economy told her they would be able to better plan around federal holidays rather than the “random” time of multiple cultural holidays.

“These are mostly people that are working hourly wages, and on those days off, they can't work,” she said. “You have families that are really struggling to make ends meet. Every day that their children are off of school is another day that their family is not earning income.”

In a statement, Loudoun County Public Schools minority committee chair Jasmine Tyler said “an inclusive calendar recognizes that our students do not all share the same traditions and holidays, but that they are important and worth observing.”

LCPS is not the only area public school system to try to alter the religious observances recognized on its school calendar. Last winter, Montgomery County Public Schools initially made Eid al-Fitr a snow make-up day, but the school board reversed the decision after community backlash.

entries.title: Ted Leonsis Named NHL Board of Governors Chairman
entries.summary: Leonsis, who owns the Capitals in addition to the Wizards and Mystics, will be taking on the highest leadership position of any NHL owner.
entries.content:
Capitals owner Ted Leonsis was unanimously elected chairman of the NHL’s Board of Governors on Tuesday, giving him the highest leadership position a league owner can have. He replaced Boston Bruins owner Jeremy Jacobs, who stepped down after 19 years in the role.

Calgary Flames owner Murray Edwards was voted to be Leonsis’ vice chairman. They will work with NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman and his deputy, Bill Daly, on an array of league-wide matters, including its upcoming media rights deal and possible expansion.

“I'm more strategy, big picture, vision, new media; Murray is operations, finance,” Leonsis told reporters Tuesday. “He reads the minutes of the reports. He understands the balance sheets. In my 28 years, the league has grown so dramatically. … Bill and Gary are a team. Murray and I and the executive committee are a team, and I think we have the opportunity to continue to have the tree grow to heaven.”

Leonsis, 69, brings a very different approach to the position compared to his predecessor. Jacobs rarely met with the media and wasn’t especially front-facing. Leonsis is among the most accessible owners in sports, including interacting with fans on social media.

“Ted Leonsis’ entrepreneurial instincts and forward-thinking approach have helped shape the direction of our league for more than two decades,” Bettman said. “Since joining the board of governors, Ted has been an invaluable leader and a thoughtful voice in our boardroom, bringing to our discussions the same innovative spirit he has poured into Monumental Sports & Entertainment.

“I am excited to work alongside him in this new capacity as we continue to build on the remarkable momentum of our league.”

Leonsis steps into the role with a few major tasks on his radar. The league has already started preparing for the 74-year old Bettman — the longest-tenured commissioner in North American professional sports as he enters his 34th season running the league — to retire, and Leonsis will likely play a major role in picking his successor.

“We haven’t been talking about succession specifically here, but it’s the most important job for a board of directors of a public company,” Leonsis said Tuesday.

The NHL is also looking into potential expansion, with Phoenix, Atlanta, Austin and Houston all under consideration. And Leonsis will also have a say in the league’s new U.S. media rights deal, which needs to be finalized before the 2028-29 season starts.

“It’s not about TV anymore,” Leonsis said. “It’s about global digital and finding the next generation of big important partners. … It’s still a huge part of our revenue base and is very, very strategic for us.”

entries.title: Zelenskyy Urges Leaders at the U.N. to Keep Choking Russia's Economy
entries.summary: “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time," the Ukrainian president said.
entries.content:
By Edith M. Lederer and Jennifer Peltz

Ukrainian President President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged the world’s leaders Wednesday to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts, telling the U.N. General Assembly that “Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said, speaking in English at the U.N. General Assembly.

Russia gets its turn Saturday to address the assembly. President Vladimir Putin hasn’t traveled to the gathering in years, sending Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov instead. Lavrov told the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday that Russia is prepared to negotiate toward a lasting peace but won’t just “pause” the war. He argued that such a pause would just buy Ukraine and its backers time to line up more weapons.

“Something always seems to stop Putin from saying, ‘That’s it. Enough, peace,’” Zelenskyy said. “Can you even imagine him without war? He is ‘Patient Zero’, the one from whom war keeps spreading further. ... ‘Patient Zero’ must be stopped."

Russia invaded Ukraine more than 4½ years ago. Western analysts estimate that over 500,000 Russian troops have been killed and that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Neither country discloses its own casualty totals.

The war has had global repercussions for fuel, fertilizer and grain shipments — and for geopolitics, widening divisions between Russia and the West.

With front-line positions in eastern and southern Ukraine largely unchanged since last year, Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range attacks with drones and missiles.

entries.title: Thune Ramps Up Spending in Texas as Paxton Struggles in Polling
entries.summary: The Senate majority leader’s political committee has now allocated nearly $119 million to broadcast advertising, far outpacing Trump’s contributions for his preferred candidate.
entries.content:
A super PAC tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune has nearly doubled its broadcast advertising efforts in Texas to support Republican Ken Paxton — bringing the group’s spending total to nearly $119 million as they try to fend off Democrat James Talarico.

The new spending on TV reservations constitutes a major jump from the $63 million Texas PAC had disclosed through Sept. 18, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact and FEC filings.

A recent rush to spend big reflects deeper party concerns about keeping a reliably red seat held by outgoing Sen. John Cornyn. It also far outpaces President Donald Trump’s super PAC contributions for the race so far this month.

Senate Republicans have rarely concentrated resources so heavily on Texas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the upper chamber since 1988 and is home to one of the country’s most expensive media markets. But recent polling indicates that Talarico, a state representative, is Democrats’ best chance at flipping a Senate seat in Texas, outpacing other recent party hopefuls like Beto O’Rourke in 2018 and former U.S. Rep. Colin Allred in 2024.

Republicans ramped up spending in the state throughout the first two weeks of September. In addition to Senate Republicans’ investment in the race, mostly concentrated on broadcast and digital advertising, Trump’s MAGA Inc. dropped $10 million at the beginning of the month — following weeks of lawmakers’ public and private pleas to the president to spend more of his war chest to support Republicans in tight races.

Thune has been the most prominent Republican encouraging Trump to get more involved in Texas, though he and other lawmakers are prohibited by campaign finance law from directing super PAC spending. He has acknowledged Paxton's race will be expensive: The Senate Leadership Fund super PAC projected that it could take up to $250 million to keep the seat red with Paxton on the ballot in November, Punchbowl reported last year, compared with a cost of $25 million to $70 million to help Cornyn win reelection.

PAC spending from Thune and Trump in Texas now heavily surpasses expenditures in the other competitive Senate races this cycle. This month, the pair have dropped roughly $30 million in Ohio to protect Sen. Jon Husted, $16.5 million for Mike Rogers in Michigan and nearly $16 million to boost Michael Whatley in North Carolina. Combined, both super PACs and adjacent branches have spent upwards of $4 million to $8 million each to support Republican candidates in Georgia, New Hampshire, Iowa and Alaska.

Thune’s committees have also boosted Sens. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska and Susan Collins in Maine, though Trump’s groups have not disclosed major spending in either race.

Sen. Tim Scott, who leads the National Republican Senatorial Committee, on Wednesday directed party members up for reelection to run like they are behind, Semafor reported. The South Carolina Republican singled out GOP-held seats like Texas and Iowa, which have seldom attracted as much spending and attention as seats in more traditional battleground states.

Entering September, the NSRC had not spent heavily in Texas, instead sending more than $10 million to Ohio and $8 million to Iowa and North Carolina last month, the political committee reported. They also spent between $1.5 million and $5 million on Republicans in New Hampshire, Michigan, Georgia, Maine, Alaska and South Carolina.

Talarico had maintained a substantial financial advantage on the airwaves before Republicans’ spending blitz this month, with the Democratic campaign spending about $31.3 million on advertising in the summer compared with Paxton’s reservations, worth just over $150,000 by the end of August. Two weeks after Labor Day, broadcast ad reservations boosting the Republican candidate now more than double the $54 million spent in Talarico’s favor, AdImpact reported.

Paxton, whom many Republicans have characterized as a weak candidate, has repeatedly and increasingly referenced Talarico’s strong poll showing in fundraising emails. Multiple pro-Paxton messages this week have highlighted the Democratic state representative’s high ActBlue small donor hauls from August, saying Talarico had “bought” every point of his polling lead.

“Ken’s ads are finally on the air,” one Sept. 22 email reads. “The momentum is real. But James Talarico is about to take that $12.98 million and pour every dollar of it into Texas television between now and November 3rd.”

But six weeks out from the midterms, some prominent Texas Republicans are keeping away. Former President George W. Bush and Cornyn, who lost to Paxton in a contentious primary runoff, held a Republican fundraiser in Dallas on Monday night to boost battleground Senate candidates — except for Paxton, who reportedly was not on the invite list.

Paxton “doesn’t need the money,” Cornyn told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the event, adding that dollars can go farther in smaller states.

“There’s a limited resource and so at some point, the powers that be are going to have to make decisions about where you spend money, and if you spend it for lost causes in some of these places that aren’t looking good,” the Texas Republican said. “Should you move that money to places where it might make a difference?”

When asked if Paxton counted as a “lost cause,” Cornyn responded, “I’m going to leave that up to the voters.”

Texas candidates have criticized Republican leadership for not spending enough in the past: Sen. Ted Cruz blasted then-Majority Leader Mitch McConnell for the political committee not directing substantial dollars to his 2024 race.

entries.title: DOJ Argues Trump Banned Three Media Outlets Over ‘National Security’ Concerns
entries.summary: The judge appeared skeptical of the government’s arguments, saying due process “wasn’t followed here.”
entries.content:
Three media outlets urged a federal judge on Wednesday to grant them a temporary restraining order blocking President Donald Trump’s decision to ban them from the White House grounds, arguing that the ban violated the First Amendment and spurred due process concerns.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration on Monday after the White House confiscated their reporters’ media badges over the weekend. The case is part of the president’s contentious history with prohibiting media access, though journalists who have had their credentials revoked have historically won in court.

The Justice Department added a new layer to Trump’s ban during the hearing, arguing that the outlets had undermined national security interests through their reporting. That reasoning was not mentioned in the president’s initial announcement post on Friday, which bashed the companies’ “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS” — a theme DOJ lawyers also repeated throughout the roughly hourlong hearing, adding that access to the White House “is a privilege, not a right.”

The media outlets’ legal team said federal law allows the president to be critical of the news, but it does not empower him to use his power to punish the journalists.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who ordered the Trump administration to restore then-CNN Chief White House Correspondent Jim Acosta’s press pass in 2018, opened the hearing by referencing D.C. federal court precedent that gives journalists the right to receive adequate notice about their conduct prior to their passes being revoked. Kelly, a Trump appointee, appeared skeptical of the government’s arguments at multiple points, and said due process “wasn’t followed here” — a constitutional guarantee that has come up in previous media cases.

Kelly said he would issue a ruling “as soon as I can,” meaning Trump’s ban will remain in effect for the dozens of journalists with White House press credentials.

On Tuesday, the Trump administration sent letters to the three companies, citing national security concerns and standards of journalistic professionalism as justification for the bans. The DOJ’s attorney, Michael Velchik, asserted that the notification sent in the letters was acceptable because “general standards of journalism professionalism are widely known.”

But the letters were sent after the initial ban, the attorney representing the media outlets, Ted Boutrous Jr., argued, characterizing them as a post-hoc justification from the administration.

“I don’t know how a letter that they got after the pass was revoked would have provided them with the kind of standard they had to conform their conduct to,” Kelly said in response to Velchik.

Boutrous said the case “all of a sudden” encompasses national security — which Trump did not mention “at all” in his initial Truth Social post on Friday. Since Trump “wears his heart on his sleeve” and often publicly criticizes members of the media and their reporting, the ban is a clear example of viewpoint discrimination, Boutrous said.

He also pointed to the broader “chilling effect” that the media ban could have “on a reasonable person or reasonable reporter.”

The DOJ published a list of stories from the outlets that prompted the ban in their court filing Tuesday night. Boutrous noted that of the four CNN articles, only one was written by a reporter with a hard pass, the type of credential that the White House revoked ahead of this case.

In regards to any viewpoint discrimination, “the president criticizes many people, probably every news organization,” Velchik said. “He has criticized other news organizations even more,” and reporters should not get a “get out of jail free card” because the president has criticized them at some point, he added.

Velchik also pointed to Friday’s 5 p.m. deadline for the journalists to submit their formal objections to White House for consideration before the administration makes the ban final, and called on Kelly to consider the potential relief that process could provide.

entries.title: Iowa Judge Tosses Trump’s Suit Against the Des Moines Register and Pollster
entries.summary: Trump's legal team is expected to appeal the decision to the Iowa Supreme Court.
entries.content:
By Hannah Fingerhut

DES MOINES, Iowa — A judge on Wednesday dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president’s claim that the newspaper’s poll coverage violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law.

Calling the case extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie said that allowing the lawsuit and its “faulty” claims to proceed could have a chilling effect that “can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs.” He sided with pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper in affirming that the poll and coverage of it were constitutionally protected political speech, not a commercial product.

The ruling Wednesday came hours after a judge heard arguments but did not rule from the bench in a case on Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. Trump banned the three outlets last Friday, assailing what he called “fake news.”

After the ruling in Iowa Wednesday, a spokesman for Trump's legal team said the president will take his case to the Iowa Supreme Court.

Trump filed the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and the newspaper’s parent company in December 2024, accusing them of fraudulently publishing inaccurate poll results to damage him and help Democrats, saying coverage of polls is not protected speech.

Trump and his team have filed several lawsuits against media organizations accusing them of bias, calling into question the boundaries of free speech protections, particularly for the press. Some of those lawsuits have ended in settlements.

In dismissing the case in Iowa state court, Beattie wrote that Trump’s lawsuit sought to “stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability.” After hearing the arguments, the judge concluded the constitutional protection “is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed.”

Beattie said the case would have to be dismissed even if, solely for the purpose of deciding the motions, he accepted the Trump team’s allegations that the poll was intentionally skewed and its results fabricated. “Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails,” the judge wrote, because the lawsuit did not meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception.

U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun, both Republicans, joined the lawsuit.

The poll, conducted by Selzer’s company in the final days of October and released just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democrats’ presidential nominee, capturing 47% of Iowa likely voters, to Trump’s 44%. Trump ultimately won the support of 56% of the nearly 2 million Iowans who voted.

Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations, valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and campaign funds and resources.

Selzer’s case was taken up by the free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. She said Wednesday she was grateful for the ruling, which “reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference.”

“Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance," Selzer said in a statement, "and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome."

entries.title: Trump Greets Xi With Red-Carpet Ceremony Ahead of State Visit
entries.summary: The leaders are expected to discuss Iran, trade and AI governance at a state dinner Thursday night.
entries.content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived to a red-carpet greeting at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday night ahead of a much-anticipated state visit with President Donald Trump.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump welcomed the Chinese delegation on the tarmac with a show of military might and pomp. A military cordon stood at attention alongside American dignitaries in front of a sprawling phalanx of F-22 and F-16 fighter jets, as B-1 bombers circled overhead.

The two leaders walked the length of the red carpet as an honor guard shot off a salute battery and the Marine Band struck up the U.S. national anthem.

The visit comes as the Trump administration steps up pressure on countries accused of supporting Iran. The two leaders are expected to discuss tensions in the Middle East at a State Dinner on Thursday night, and are hoping to make progress on a deal establishing a new bilateral trade board coupled with some tariff relief.

A discussion on AI governance is also likely: Prominent technology industry leaders are expected to attend, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and SpaceX and Tesla founder Elon Musk, according to a senior U.S. official.

entries.title: China Is Holding Sensitive F-35 Parts That Were Meant to Be Shipped to the U.S.
entries.summary: The parts contain material designed to hide the fighter jet from radar, which could help China study the technology.
entries.content:
The Chinese government is holding sensitive F-35 parts that were inexplicably diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the United States,Bloomberg reported Wednesday.

The parts contain material designed to hide the fighter jet from radar, according to the report.

The report broke as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a multi-day state visit and talks with President Donald Trump.

UPS was transporting a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door from an Australian military F-35 to the U.S. in late May. The parts were being sent for inspection and possible repair or disposal. The shipment stopped in South Korea before being routed to Hong Kong.

It remains unclear whether the diversion was deliberate or accidental.

The Chinese government later took possession of the parts. The Pentagon had previously acknowledged the components were missing, but it had not said Beijing possessed them.

Congress has been investigating the incident for months. State Department and Pentagon officials first briefed congressional staff in June.

Australia’s defense minister confirmed the diversion Tuesday but said he did not believe the shipment contained sensitive parts. Lockheed Martin, which manufactures the fighter jets, said the components were unserviceable and posed little risk of exploitation.

Bloomberg’s report raises new questions about those assessments. Both parts were coated with radar-absorbing material that helps conceal the aircraft from enemy detection.

Physical access could help China study the material, check information obtained through espionage or improve systems designed to detect the F-35.

The incident could also intensify congressional scrutiny of Trump’s proposed sale of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia.

The State Department notified Congress last week of a potential $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35s, 49 engines and related equipment to Riyadh. Congress has 30 days to review the deal.

U.S. intelligence agencies have warned that China could obtain F-35 technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or through its growing military and security relationship with the kingdom.

entries.title: Flock Changes Search Rules Ahead of Senate Hearing on Privacy Concerns
entries.summary: Democrats and Republicans broadly agreed that, in the wrong hands, the devices could be used to target everyone from gun owners to people seeking abortion care.
entries.content:
Flock Safety sought to ease growing alarm over its controversial mass surveillance tools Wednesday ahead of a Senate hearing on its technology.

In a letter to Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri), chair of the Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, the company said it had tightened rules around how law enforcement officers can search its vast databases of images of people in their vehicles.

The company’s chief legal officer said Flock is now requiring subscribers to provide a specific reason for their queries. Previously, subscribers could enter any justification they wanted in a “free-text” field.

Hawley said this made it difficult to hold people accountable for unjustified searches — in some cases, he said, subscribers had simply entered “search” or “LOL.”

“Flock admitted that until very recently, there were basically no curbs or restrictions on which of these subscribers, so to speak, could search their databases, what they could do with the images, how long the images were kept, or what other uses they were put to,” Hawley said at Wednesday’s hearing.

In the hearing, titled “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” Hawley and other lawmakers warned about the potential for AI-powered camera networks operated by Flock and other technology companies to violate the constitutional and privacy rights of millions of innocent Americans.

Flock alone has deployed 120,000 cameras on roads in every state but Hawaii, vacuuming up huge quantities of data on motorists. Other companies have deployed similar devices.

“If you haven’t heard of Flock,” Hawley said, “all I have to say is, Flock has probably heard of you.”

Hawley invited the chief executives of Flock, Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions, and Verkada to testify. All declined.

“Obviously they’re nervous about being on camera,” Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) quipped at the beginning of the discussion.

The hearing showcased bipartisan interest in regulating Flock’s cameras and similar technologies, with Democrats and Republicans broadly agreeing that, in the wrong hands, the devices could be used to target everyone from gun owners to people seeking abortion care.

Privacy experts from the American Civil Liberties Union and the Institute for Justice testified, along with a cybersecurity engineer who has exposed vulnerabilities in Flock’s systems and Lindsey Isaacs, a Florida motorist who was wrongfully accused of causing a fatal car crash based partially on Flock data.

An Ariziona sheriff who recently canceled his county’s contract with Flock also spoke, calling for “clear, statutory boundaries” on the technology, which he said encroaches too deeply on American’s constitutional rights.

“If my deputies need a search warrant to put a physical tracker on a vehicle, where is the line for camera systems that build an identical, AI-driven map of a citizen’s life?” Sheriff Ross Teeple testified.

At the hearing’s conclusion, Hawley displayed a quote from Flock CEO Garrett Langley saying Americans had “already given up the traditional sense of privacy” in exchange for greater safety.

“Do you want to make that trade-off? Are we going to live in a world where we may all have to suffer the deprivations that Ms. Isaacs did because some robot decides we were at the scene of a crime?” Hawley asked. “I suggest to you that this viewpoint is the problem.”

entries.title: Oil and Gas Industry Urges Trump to Resist a Diesel Export Ban
entries.summary: Some congressional Republicans facing increasingly tough elections this November have called on Trump to enact an export ban.
entries.content:
The country’s most powerful oil, gas and business groups urged President Donald Trump on Wednesday against pursuing any form of diesel export ban, as reports circulated that the White House is increasingly interested in finding a way to tamp sky-high diesel prices.

“We urge you to reject calls to ban or otherwise limit the exports of diesel and other products that have made the U.S. energy industry so strong,” dozens of industry groups, including the American Petroleum Institute, the American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, the National Association of Manufacturers and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, wrote in a letter to the president.

“Export bans would lead to less fuel production, tighter supplies, and rising costs for American families, farmers, and truckers,” the groups wrote.

Before now, the American Petroleum Institute has been an especially stalwart champion of the Trump administration’s energy policies and has rarely offered any public rebuke of the president. But the prospect of a temporary export ban has prompted fierce opposition from industry groups.

Politico reported Wednesday that the White House is preparing a temporary export ban on diesel. The White House denied any such preparations, but some congressional Republicans facing increasingly tough elections this November have called on Trump to enact an export ban to address rising energy prices caused by his war with Iran. Farm state Republicans, already feeling the heat from constituents over the administration’s trade wars, have also been calling for a quick fix on diesel.

“I hope WH doesnt listen 2 Big Oil who claim diesel export ban wont work Big Oil doesnt need 2 charge sky-high diesel prices 4 Iowa farmers + truckers just filling up,” Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who has endorsed the idea of a ban, posted on X Wednesday.

Opposition to an export ban extends to Trump’s own cabinet. Both Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Energy Secretary Chris Wright have repeatedly dismissed calls from lawmakers for the ban.

“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn't work," Wright said at a Climate Week event in New York on Wednesday. "If you can't ⁠export the diesel that comes out of our refineries, you run out of places to store it, and you have to reduce U.S. refining, which would ⁠put upward pressure on gasoline prices and jet fuel prices.”

Burgum expressed a similar sentiment earlier this month.

“We would consider an export ban if we thought that actually might lower prices, but that's not the case,” Burgum said at a G20 ministerial meeting in mid-September.

Diesel export bans are wildly unpopular with the oil and gas industry and with market observers, who generally agree that limits on diesel exports would lead to higher gasoline prices for consumers in the long run.

The diesel market is a global one, with U.S. producers exporting about 30% of what they produce. A ban on exporting diesel to the rest of the world would likely cause domestic producers to cut their production rates, analysts said.

Because diesel and gasoline are produced together, cuts in diesel production could also mean cuts in gasoline production, which would eventually transfer to higher gas prices at the pump.

“If exports are banned, refiners cannot simply stockpile unlimited diesel. They would have to reduce production. Because gasoline and diesel are produced together, producing less diesel also means producing less gasoline,” said an AFPM spokesperson in a statement. “Less fuel production means tighter supplies and higher prices for both diesel and gasoline.”

The ban would likely hurt the Northeast part of the country the most. “Areas of the U.S. that import fuel (primarily the Northeast) would face higher prices for all fuels that would now be in even shorter supply globally. This could not come at a worse time for consumers as home heating oil season is about to begin,” the business groups wrote in their letter.

The United States had a crude oil export ban from 1975 until 2015, when Congress repealed the ban. Since 2015, U.S. oil production has dramatically increased, and the U.S. has transitioned from primarily a petroleum products importer to primarily an exporter. Because the U.S. now supplies the global market, any global export ban would also have a serious ripple effect on prices around the world.

“The bottom line is this: the U.S. is not short of diesel. The world is. A potential export ban treats the global price problem as if it was a U.S. only problem,” wrote Patrick De Haan, the petroleum analyst known as Gas Buddy.

entries.title: It Pays to Be ‘Proud to Be an American’
entries.summary: A federal ethics filing by Lee Greenwood’s wife, made after her ambassador nomination, shows the MAGA star has racked up royalty checks for Trump’s favorite song.
entries.content:
The musician Lee Greenwood, President Donald Trump’s unofficial MAGA troubadour, earned up to $1 million in recent months from his song “God Bless the USA,” which the president routinely plays at political events and appearances.

Greenwood’s wife, Kimberly Greenwood, whom Trump nominated earlier this month as ambassador to Barbados and several other Caribbean island nations, disclosed her husband’s income stream in a new federal ethics filing, covering the months between June 2025 and June 2026.

The ethics filing also indicates that Lee Greenwood earned between $100,001 and $1 million in payments related to sales of the “God Bless the USA Bible” — marketed as the “only Bible endorsed” by both Trump and Greenwood.

While “God Bless the USA” easily stands as Lee Greenwood’s most lucrative recording in recent months, he also earned smaller royalty payments from several other songs in his extensive catalog, including renditions of patriotic standards “Battle Hymn of the Republic” and “The Star-Spangled Banner” (up to $1,000 each). The Greenwoods are only required by law to disclose income amounts in broad ranges.

Lee Greenwood’s all-but-forgotten recording of “God Bless Canada” — a 1989 adaptation of “God Bless the USA” that the musician recorded at then-President George H.W. Bush’s behest — also earned the singer up to $1,000 in recent months amid diplomatic and trade disputes between the United States and Canada.

The song includes the lyrics:From the shores of Nova Scotia / To the forest in BC / From Montreal to Winnipeg / From sea to shining sea / From Detroit we can see her / Above the USA / ’Cause there’s pride in every Canadian heart / And it’s time to stand and say

Lee Greenwood also earned “monetization payments” from Facebook, X and the custom video platform Cameo, according to his wife’s filing, which did not specify income amounts.

A representative for Lee Greenwood could not immediately be reached for comment.Lee Greenwood has personally performed alongside Trump on numerous occasions, including at the president’s 2025 inauguration festivities, the July 4 celebration this year in Washington and earlier this month at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas.

Kimberly Greenwood herself reported owning an extensive stock and financial investment portfolio worth millions of dollars.In a federal ethics agreement Kimberly Greenwood signed Sept. 4, she pledged to “not participate personally and substantially” in matters that have a “direct and predictable effect on Lee Greenwood Inc.,” her husband’s entertainment company.

She also pledged to resign her position with Greenwood Productions Inc. and “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest” if confirmed as ambassador, according to the agreement.

entries.title: Trump Administration Publicly Invites Putin to Attend the G20 Summit
entries.summary: If the Russian leader attends, it will be the first time he has gone in person since 2019.
entries.content:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that the U.S. invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami this December, after Rubio spoke with another Russian official on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday.

“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio told reporters. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”

If Putin goes to the summit in December, it will mark the first time he has attended the geopolitical meeting in person since 2019. Russia has maintained its status as a G20 member nation throughout the country’s four-year-long war with Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces recently launched aggressive strikes against Russian oil refineries, and The Financial Times reported that Trump urged Zelenskyy over the weekend to halt the attacks in order to ease global strain on gas and diesel prices — a crisis that has been compounded by the Iran war and the conflict over the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio said that both Russia and Ukraine are interested in a limited ceasefire.

“Both sides have expressed an interest in some limited ceasefire that involved grain and energy. Obviously, you know, that won't be easy either,” Rubio said.

Rubio reportedly spoke with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Wednesday to extend the invitation for December. The invitation comes days after Trump signed a sweeping bipartisan Russian sanctions bill aimed at increasing economic pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.

Multiple Senate Republicans criticized the Trump administration’s decision to publicly call for Putin to attend the G20 summit.

“Putin should not be invited to [the] G20 summit,” Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts, who sits on the Foreign Relations Committee, told The Washington Sun. “He is prosecuting a war in Ukraine right now, and we should treat him like the dictator he is.”

Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker, chair of Senate Armed Services Committee, said he “wouldn’t have done it,” while Texas Sen. John Cornyn called the invitation a “bad idea.”

Sen. Todd Young said an invitation would make sense only if Putin were prepared to make major concessions.

“I think elevating Vladimir Putin is not where we should be focused right now,” the Indiana Republican said. “We should be trying to come up with ways to bring him to the table for a serious negotiation.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), who championed the sanctions bill alongside the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, called the invitation “absolutely disgraceful, despicable.”

“I’m hoping for tougher action and expecting it because he signed the bill and supported it.” Blumenthal told The Washington Sun.

Rubio’s announcement “makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine,” Democrats from the House Foreign Affairs Committee wrote in an X post Wednesday.

entries.title: D.C. Council Proposal Would Allow Businesses to Hire Off-Duty Parking Officers
entries.summary: The bill mirrors a program that allows businesses to hire MPD officers to patrol around their properties.
entries.content:
In an effort to crack down on highly congested streets, the D.C. Council is considering a bill that would allow business groups, universities and event organizers to hire off-duty parking-enforcement officers to patrol around their properties.

The bill, introduced by Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau, would allow the Department of Public Works to let officers work as a reimbursable detail for eligible organizations, which would pay the department for the time served.

The model mirrors the District’s arrangement with the Metropolitan Police Department allowing businesses to hire police officers.

“In addition to keeping our streets calmer and safer,” Nadeau said, “these arrangements will allow us to improve parking enforcement in hot spots and congested areas and ensure that the parking system enables a rotation of vehicles in and out of commercial neighborhoods like it’s designed to.”

Campus and special police officers would also be allowed to work as part of the reimbursable details, but only in and around their jurisdiction. The bill overrides a regulation that prevents some campus and special police departments from enforcing city parking restrictions, Nadeau said.

The bill drew pushback from At-Large council member Robert White, who said residents aren’t as worried about parking enforcement as they are about how much parking tickets cost.

“I hear so frequently from residents that they are just being killed by the number and size of parking fees,” White said. “I continue to be concerned that the city uses tickets as a source of revenue rather than safety and fidelity of laws."

Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George echoed White's concern, saying the reimbursement detail model should have been tested before being signed into law.

“I would love for us to have piloted it first before moving forward with permanent legislation,” she said, “and I think that’s probably the most prudent thing that we should do, and so my lack of support is because I think this does deserve a little more testing.”

The bill passed its first reading with seven “yes” votes and three “no” votes from White, Lewis George and Ward 7 council member Wendell Felder.

At-Large council member Christina Henderson and Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker voted “present.” Ward 8 council member Trayon White was absent.

The second reading and final vote of the bill are expected to take place in October.
